A proper return to Westeros - I stayed up for the 3 am UK premiere and, after one episode, it is already clear that this is a significant improvement over House of the Dragon. I never actually bothered finishing the second season of HotD as it just didn't grab me, but I loved the original Game of Thrones and have read all the books. Already, I feel this new series captures that early GoT vibe.

The casting is excellent so far. Peter Claffey is appropriately tall for Ser Dunk. Beyond just the physical presence, there is more humour here that was sorely missing from House of the Dragon. The production values are magnificent; the scenery, costumes, and the general grittiness of the setting feel authentic, as you would expect with such a high-budget production.

It is obviously too early to give a definitive verdict on the whole season, but having read the book years ago, I already know the story is good. The narrative is much less convoluted than the main books, which makes it easy to stick to the simple and fun plot. What I've seen so far stays close to the text, which is always a good sign for long-time fans. If they maintain this level of quality and focus on the character dynamics, this should be a major hit with the original Game of Thrones fanbase. It's the most "at home" I've felt in Westeros for a long time.

avis:
Really freaking good with only one bad moment (so far) - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, based on the first episode, seems to be a return to the parts of GoT that were completely missing from the last couple seasons: a good script, well-written characters, and a sense of realism. While the show is surely more lighthearted than its predecessor, it still feels like part of the same universe that existed from first few seasons, unlike the slop that was season 8. It allows the plot some room to breathe and pace itself properly. Some might call it slow, but for me, that was not the case; again, it's very reminiscent of seasons 1-3 in terms of how much of the screentime is spent building up the world it's in. I would even say it's tonally similar to Arya and The Hound's adventures within those seasons.

On to the specifics: the main character, Dunk, is a bit of an oaf, but one with a heart of gold, who has a sense of duty and a wisdom that is unseen in most of the characters we've come across in Westeros. We don't see much of his companion, Egg, in the first episode, but it's clear that he has a similar heart and a complete lack of life experience, making him both naïve and endearing. Both are well-acted and have great chemistry on-screen, and the same can be said for the other, more minor characters introduced so far.

The only bad scene of the episode comes within the first five minutes, a bit which employs immature potty humor as a way to shock the viewers into a cheap laugh. I was not a fan of it at all, and in fact, I considered not watching the rest of the episode because of it, but I'm glad I did, as the other 39 minutes were pure gold. If the show leans too much into the toilet humor in the future, I fear it will follow the same fate as season 8 and quickly fade into irrelevance. If the rest of the show is more like the other 39 minutes, I have no doubt that this will redeem HBO after Game of Thrones' disappointing final season.

The Refreshing of Seven Kingdom - I can sense the potential of this show Honestly, it was refreshing to watch. It doesn't try too hard to shock you or drown everything in politics and cruelty like most Westeros stuff. It's slower, quieter, and way more personal-and that's exactly why I liked it.

Ser Duncan the Tall is such a good change from the usual smart-but-evil or powerful-but-broken characters. He's not special in the flashy way. He messes up, doubts himself, and clearly doesn't even know if he deserves to be a knight half the time. But he keeps trying anyway, and that makes him super easy to root for. Watching him slowly try to live up to his potential instead of magically becoming great overnight felt real.

Then there's Egg. Their relationship is easily the best part of the story. It's weirdly wholesome for Westeros. Egg is curious, sharp, and clearly more than he seems, while Dunk is just this big guy with a strong moral compass trying to do the right thing. Their back-and-forth feels natural, not forced, and gives the story actual heart.

The best thing is the scale. No "save the world" nonsense. Just small conflicts, honor, and choices that matter to the people involved. It proves you don't need dragons or constant bloodshed to make Westeros interesting.

Fantasy From the Road, Not the Throne - This review covers only the first episode.

This prequel opens with a burial and ends under the stars. In between, it quietly announces what kind of story this is going to be. Not a saga about who rules. Not a prophecy machine. Not an argument about destiny. It's a story about how to behave when none of that is available to you.

That choice alone sets it apart from Game of Thrones, which told history from the throne outward. This series tells it from the road. Power here isn't something you wield. It's something you brush up against, overhear, survive, or avoid. That shift in scale changes everything.

The protagonist is a squire who claims to be a knight. We're given no paperwork, no witnesses, no ceremony. There's only a flashback of a boy serving a knight who is now dead, and a present-tense insistence on living up to something that may or may not have been formally granted. The show doesn't rush to clarify this because it doesn't matter in the way we've been trained to expect. The question isn't "Is he really a knight?" It's "What does he do when no one can confirm it?"

That ambiguity is the engine. Historically, it's accurate. Knighthood wasn't always a clean ritual with trumpets and seals. Especially outside courts, legitimacy often followed conduct rather than preceding it. Literarily, this puts the show closer to Sir Gawain and the Green Knight or Don Quixote than to epic fantasy. Identity here is something you practice until it either becomes real or collapses under pressure.

The opening scenes struck me as making the argument in physical terms. He keeps bumping into doorways because he's too tall for them. He stands watching a fake dragon in a tent and looks out of place. The world he's entering has been redesigned for people willing to stoop. The ideals he's trying to live by are larger than the spaces that now pretend to hold them. That's not a gag. That's storytelling through physics. And the humor? Sharp. Purposeful. Exactly the kind that lands when you least expect it. The dancing, the food flying, the mockery at the table. It's hilarious because it's recognizable. Power humiliates at the margins. Humiliation rarely comes as decrees; it arrives as laughter. The test isn't strength. It's humiliation tolerance. Will he lash out, shrink, perform smallness, or keep his center? Turns out, decency gets tested not when you're in danger ~ but when you're just plain embarrassed.

I think one of the smartest moves was to give the protagonist a squire of his own almost immediately. It grounds the story morally. I was not watching a man test an ideal in private. I was watching someone else learn from him in real time. Honor stops being abstract and becomes inheritance. Whatever he does next will be copied.

This is also a series that remembers bodies exist. After burial and reflection comes biology. Hunger, fatigue, and yes, bodily functions interrupting thought. Medieval literature did this constantly. The point wasn't to debase, but to test whether they could survive the flesh. If virtue can't live inside a body, it isn't virtue. It's theater.

Historically, this perspective matters. We romanticize eras by imagining ourselves as royals. In reality, almost all of us would have lived hand to mouth, without safety nets, without guarantees, without second chances. This series restores that scale. History stops being pageantry and becomes endurance. Chivalry isn't a system you benefit from. It's a belief you try to live by while the world makes it inconvenient.

The episode ends exactly where it should. Not with recognition, but with continuity. He finds the boy. He takes responsibility. He sleeps under the stars. There's no hall, no applause, no proof. Just a choice to continue. The boy (aka his squire) he finds isn't a promise. Not quite. It's a maybe a possibility with no guarantee, no safety net.

If Game of Thrones asked who should rule, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms asks how to live when ruling isn't an option. That's a quieter question. It's also a deeper one.

So far, this series isn't interested in epic spectacle or moral certainty. It's interested in decency without dignity, belief without validation, and ethics at human scale. That may disappoint viewers waiting for dragons and coups. For anyone interested in what fantasy can do beyond power fantasies, it feels like a remarkably confident beginning ~ at least for now.

The show isn't asking you to admire the past.

It's asking whether you'd recognize yourself in it.

I'm giving the first episode a 10 for its confidence, restraint, and clarity of purpose. The cast is stellar and the protagonist is solidly authentic.

avis:
"A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" - A Welcome Step Back to What Made Thrones Work - Two episodes in, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms already feels like a breath of fresh air. After the messy end of Game of Thrones and the hit-or-miss highs of House of the Dragon, this show goes smaller, quieter, and honestly smarter. It's not about power grabs or endless scheming. It's about people trying to do the right thing in a rough world.

The real strength so far is the relationship between Dunk (Peter Claffey) and Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell). Their chemistry just works. Dunk is kind, awkward, and trying his best. Egg is sharp, curious, and clearly more than he lets on. Watching them travel together feels natural and genuinely enjoyable, which is something this universe has been missing for a while.

The pacing is slower, but in a good way. Scenes aren't rushed. You get time to sit with conversations, take in the tournaments, and feel the road between places. There's still politics in the background - this is Westeros, after all - but it doesn't drown out the story.

What really stood out is how grounded everything feels. You see the struggle for money, food, and shelter. Westeros feels lived-in again, not just like a backdrop for big speeches and dragons. The sets and costumes look worn and real, which helps a lot.

If you've read the Dunk and Egg stories, this feels faithful without being stiff. It keeps the heart of the books while filling things out in a way that makes sense for TV.

So far, this doesn't feel like just another spinoff. It feels like a reset - a reminder that this world works best when it focuses on character, not spectacle. Early days, but it's a strong start and easily the most hopeful I've felt about the franchise in years.

avis: The Jury is waiting for more information - The latest in offerings a la George R. R. Martin(The R's are decidedly not for Ronald Reuel) 'begins' at least, as a buddy travelogue. Set a century before the events of 'GOT' Peter Claffey's former squire 'Dunc' sets out to discover his fortune at the death of his former master Ser Arlan of Pennytree. Having donned a knights title the first episode has him meet his own future squire Dexter Sol Ansell's 'Egg' at a wayside Inn. Originally shunning the overtures of Egg to engage him he heads on to the next market town intending to participate in a knights' tournament only to discover that in order to enlist he will need the references of an established knight or lord. We meet several players in this first foray which, to be honest is something less than a taster. Of course it is early days, and one hopes that the detectable air of tweeness is only in the way of a teaser. avis:
Without a master and without a home - So, the main character is Duncan the Tall, a knight of the Seven Kingdoms. From the very first scenes, we are shown how he buries his master, and completely alone in this world, he begins his journey. And the first thing that comes to his mind is to go to a knightly tournament, where one can earn a little money and, perhaps, gain fame. If he performs well and defeats other knights, local lords - and not only local ones, who have gathered from all across the Seven Kingdoms - may hire him into their service. And this is how he can begin his brilliant career as a knight.

Well, the events here take place a hundred years before Game of Thrones. Roughly speaking, if my memory serves me right, and if we compare it to our own world, without the presence of major dragons, it would be somewhere around the year 1200. This is already quite a late Middle Ages. It is not the 7th or 8th century, but the series is very good.

The atmosphere of the first episode - the costumes, makeup, hairstyles - is impressive. The only thing is that for now there are no particularly beautiful suits of armor. We see small tents near the city, and there are no huge medieval castles a la England, Scotland, or Ireland. And there are no shiny, elegant armors like those worn by Jaime Lannister. For now, everything looks rather modest, but despite this, let us hope that as the series goes on, it will only get better - more epic, more dazzling, with large-scale battles and scenes.

I also want to point out that, as I understand it, the story here will be told mainly from the perspective of a single knight. Because if we recall Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon, the story constantly jumped from one corner of the Seven Kingdoms to another - Winterfell, King's Landing, the Riverlands, Lannisport. avis:
Lack-luster opener with low brow "humor" - I hoped this wouldn't just be another lesser quality attempt to ride the previously successful original G.o.T. Bandwagon, but "hope" seems a pointless effort in the 21st century & that certainly appears more & more true when it comes to HBO & it is certainly true here.

These days most would agree that we're being conditioned to accept FAR LESS for the same (if you're lucky), or HIGHER prices. This series seems to be yet another embodiment of that & just another attempt to "slap a sticker" of a name brand item on an inferior quality product.

Some will say it's too early to really be so critical, but when you're riding on the success of a far more involved endeavor in the same vein of something that was so highly praised (until season 8) you really need to deliver far more in the subsequent sequel, or prequel (as in this case) introduction than you will see in the first episode of "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms."

Now, I'm not one who is of the mind that, "NOTHING will EVER beat the original G.o.T" even if I wouldn't expect that anything would.

However, I do believe that the premiere of any connected series which relies on, or claims to use, the author's original written works, should be of a caliber that is at least in the general neighborhood of it's predecessor(s).

The dynamic between the two main characters is good. The costumes, settings (although far more sparse due to local of the scenes) seem "quality" & the acting, direction & camera work are all what would & should be expected.

Unfortunately the story is dull, or as the elites of the Seven Kingdoms might say, "Boring."

While there are moments that will elicit a chuckle, or two & we all need to remember that they are establishing the groundwork that will be more fundamental to build on later, it still feels like, "there's sawdust in the bread."

While I do in fact want every & any sequel, or prequel, connected to G.o.T., to be a great success, not only due to my love of the original, but because there has always been a resoundingly near non-existent amount of quality fantasy films, or T. V. (with obvious exceptions; eg. L.o.t. R. series) series within the genre, I just can't accept another case of a corporate megalith handing us a sad & sorry little 1/8 lb. Smashed, reheated pancake of a burger & trying to convince us it's a "Quarter pounder" just because the commercial says so.

Regardless of my initial statement I still remain hopeful the series will improve.

No Dragons Required: The Quiet Power of Westeros at Street Level - If Game of Thrones was a feast with greasy fingers, goblets of wine, blood on the tablecloth and House of the Dragon was a genealogy lesson delivered with a flamethrower, then A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a roadside stew in a dented pot. Humble. Honest. Surprisingly soulful.

This isn't the story of kings who believe themselves gods. It's about a tall, decent hedge knight with more courage than coin, and a bald kid who looks like he should be selling turnips but carries the weight of dynasties in his back pocket. The stakes are smaller no apocalyptic ice storms, no dragon-on-dragon aerial dogfights but somehow they feel bigger. Personal. Human.

The genius here is restraint. Where House of the Dragon often strained under the operatic burden of its own importance, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms breathes. It wanders dusty roads. It lingers in taverns. It lets conversations simmer. You can smell the ale, the horse sweat, the damp wool. This is Westeros at eye level.

And that's the trick it remembers that before the Iron Throne was a meme, before dragons were CGI centerpieces, this world worked because of people. Flawed, funny, stubborn people trying to do one decent thing in a system designed to crush decency.

It's a worthy successor to Game of Thrones not because it tries to outdo it, but because it refuses to. No desperate escalation. No louder, bigger, bloodier. Just craft. Character. A quiet confidence that story still matters more than spectacle.

In an age of prequels that feel like corporate obligations, this one feels like someone actually cared. A breath of fresh air rolling in from the Reach, carrying with it the radical notion that fantasy can still surprise you by being simple, by being human, by being good.

avis:
A light on the gray - Pop culture is often like a pendulum that swings to the extremes, or Newtonian physics where every action has an equal and opposite reaction. After George R. R. Martin tapped late 20th century fantasy on the shoulder and told it to step aside, it was inevitable that someday the favor would be returned. Ironically, that favor was returned by Martin himself.

'A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms' is just what this saga needed right now. Heck, the genre or pop culture at large even. It needed heroes with heart and a desire to do good just for the sake of it. Make no mistake, this is still that same gray and cynical world from 'Game of Thrones' and 'House of the Dragon', but the differences here are that the complex political machinations are pushed into the background for a simpler story and that it features a pair of unlikely protagonists who push back some of that gray with their inner light.

Peter Claffey and Dexter Sol Ansell are absolutely brilliant together. They've got an old school "buddy cop" kind of chemistry that you just can't teach. It really emphasizes the importance of strong casting, because I can't see this working even half as well without them.

I love Martin's fantasy world, though in a real world gone mad, I yearn for a return to the epic heroism of old. 'A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms' may not be that exactly, but it is a nice palate cleanser between the dark and gloomy storytelling malaise of the 21st century.

adapting George R.R. Martin's beloved "Dunk and Egg" - That's such a great way to put it - and honestly, it captures exactly why A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms feels so refreshing.

It's still Westeros, but it's Westeros at ground level. Instead of massive political chess matches like in Game of Thrones, we're following two travelers on dusty roads, stopping at tourneys and villages, dealing with problems that feel immediate and human rather than world-shattering. The scale is smaller, but the emotional stakes feel just as real.

The heart of it, of course, is the partnership between Dunk and Egg. Dunk's earnest, slightly out-of-his-depth sense of honor pairs perfectly with Egg's sharp intelligence and barely contained royal confidence. Their dynamic carries the story - it's funny, warm, occasionally tense, and always grounded in genuine affection. That "medieval buddy road trip" energy gives the series a charm that's rare in this world.

Even the humor, while sometimes a touch exaggerated, works in the story's favor. It keeps the tone from tipping into the relentless bleakness that defines much of A Song of Ice and Fire. Instead of grim inevitability, there's room for awkwardness, growth, and hope.

What makes it especially compelling is how personal everything feels. Dunk isn't trying to save kingdoms - he's trying to be a good knight. Egg isn't maneuvering for power - he's learning what kind of king he wants to become. That intimacy gives the series its warmth, and that warmth makes it deeply addictive.

It's still Westeros - but it's Westeros with heart.

Saying all of that, this is easily the best series of the three in my humble opinion. The episodes are shorter, which make them faster paced, but despite having less time, the character development is absolutely superb. Although I found it took numerous seasons to develop empathy and endearment with the GOT or House characters, in only four short episodes, you find yourself absolutely endeared to both Sir Duncan and Egg. You really root for them and can empathize with the burdens of their past, weaknesses they are attempting to overcome, and relentless desire to make a better future. I think the audience will really see a lot of themselves in these two character and the story line is absolutely riveting. Moreover, it's a true underdog series.

There is also a lot of genuinely funny comedy that's also unique to this series. Although I thought the opening of episode 1 was one of the best introductions to any show in the past decade, each episode is getting better than the last. Episode 4 truly deserves the 9.6 rating it's anchieved, and I have a feeling episode 5 will be a 9.9 and probably on par with the red wedding, or maybe even eclipsing it.

This will probably go down on a lot of top 10 lists of greatest shows of all time. At least top 20 ;).

Do yourself a favor and watch. It's the best GOT yet!

avis:
The Series That Proves Westeros Isn't About Power, it's About Heart - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" isn't just a prequel to the epic saga we all thought we knew, it's a revelation. From the very first scene, the series invites you into a Westeros you've never truly explored: quieter, more intimate, yet just as dangerously compelling. Here, honor isn't measured by crowns or armies, but by the choices one makes in the shadows, in moments no one else witnesses.

Podrick Payne and Ser Duncan the Tall are more than characters; they are mirrors reflecting the enduring struggle between morality and survival. Every conversation crackles with wit, tension, and a subtle wisdom that reminds us why tales of knighthood have captivated generations. The cinematography deserves a standing ovation: the sweeping landscapes, the claustrophobic taverns, the flickering torchlight, all feel meticulously crafted to pull viewers into a living, breathing medieval world.

But what truly sets this series apart is its humanity. Unlike the grand spectacle of battles and dragons, "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" revels in the small moments, the awkward courtship, the moral dilemmas, the fleeting acts of kindness. It whispers the timeless truth that heroism is not always loud or glorious; sometimes, it's simply choosing to do the right thing when no one is watching.

In an era of high-octane fantasy, this show is a meditation on patience, honor, and friendship. It reminds us that Westeros isn't only about power, it's about people, choices, and the legacies they leave behind. For anyone who's ever longed to see the soul of the Seven Kingdoms laid bare, this series is essential viewing.

A Mixed Bag of Chivalry, Stalling, and Bot-Fueled Tens - The journey from Flea Bottom to Ashford is a bumpy ride that struggles to find a consistent gear.

What started as a sluggish, almost aimless wander eventually ignited into a high-stakes blockbuster by the mid-season, only to fizzle out with a finale that felt more like a chore than a conclusion.

The show captures the rustic charm of the books but inherits their pacing issues, often mistaking "atmospheric" for "filler." While the chemistry between Dunk and Egg is the undeniable anchor, the season is marred by a strange disconnect... from the manufactured 10/10 pre-release hype to the uneven distribution of narrative weight. It's a series that shines when the steel clangs and the royal secrets unravel, but far too often, it's content to just stall in the mud.

7/10: A decent start, but Season 2 needs more than just a destination; it needs a pulse. An I won't be getting on that train without "genuine" reviews.

Great Casting, Small Budget, Too Many Toilet Jokes - The Show absolutely nails the Song of Ice and Fire atmosphere. From the very first episode, it genuinely feels like this story belongs in the Game of Thrones world. It is a smaller, more intimate tale that understands the rules, and moral ambiguity of Westeros.

The casting is one of the show's strongest elements. Everyone fits naturally into the world, but Dexter Sol Ansell in particular stands out.

That said, the show isn't without its problems.

My biggest issue is the toilet humor. I hate toilet humor, and for some reason American productions seem to love it. What makes this worse is that the creators openly justify it. In the behind-the-scenes documentary, they explain that adding toilet jokes makes the show more lighthearted and funny. There's even a table read where the line "the character has watery diarrhea" (this gets also shown) gets read aloud-and everyone bursts out laughing

The short format doesn't help either. With episodes clocking in at only 30 minutes, the pacing often feels rushed. Combine that with just six episodes total, and the season probably will end before it really has time to breathe.

The reduced budget is noticeable. While the show still looks great, you can clearly tell this isn't operating on the same financial level as Game of Thrones or House of the Dragon. Fewer locations, smaller-scale scenes, and restrained spectacle all hint at tighter production limits.

avis:
A Love Letter to The Knight of the Seven Kingdoms - The Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a rare and beautiful thing in the world of Westeros: a story that chooses kindness. It treats its source material with deep respect, but more importantly, it treats its characters-especially its simplest one-with profound dignity.

Dunk is not a chosen one, not a political mastermind, not a dragon-rider or a king. He is just a man trying, earnestly and stubbornly, to do the right thing in a world that barely notices such efforts. Watching him strive to be honorable in a landscape defined by indifference, cruelty, and social hierarchy is quietly powerful. His heroism doesn't come from destiny or brilliance, but from decency-and that makes it feel earned in a way few fantasy stories manage.

The Battle of the Seven is a standout moment not because it is flashy, but because it is real. The choreography is grounded, brutal, and emotionally weighted. Every movement reflects exhaustion, fear, and resolve. You can feel the chaos, the confusion, and the sheer physical toll of combat, making the outcome feel uncertain and painfully human until the very end.

But at the heart of the story lies the remarkable parallel between Dunk's relationship with his master, Ser Arlan, and his own bond with Egg. The first shapes him; the second reveals who he has become. Arlan's quiet and weird mentorship forms the foundation of Dunk's sense of honor, and even in death his presence lingers in every decision Dunk makes. In many ways, Dunk unconsciously becomes for Egg what Arlan once was for him. The guidance he received is now reflected in the way he protects, teaches, and shapes the young boy beside him. The parallel is deeply moving. It's a reminder that true mentorship, grounded in quiet honor, can outlive death and continue to guide others long after the mentor is gone.

Ultimately, The Knight of the Seven Kingdoms shines because it understands that greatness doesn't always need to be huge. Sometimes it already there by choosing goodness simply because someone once taught it that this is what a knight should be. And in doing so, it tells one of the most human stories the world of Westeros has ever offered.

Ansell handles it with charm, timing, and just enough mischief to make it all feel natural.

Honestly, if this performance is any indication of where he's headed, it feels less like an introduction and more like the opening chapter of a career that's going to end up collecting a few trophies along the way.

Very great show - "What a great show" feels like the most natural opening line when talking about A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, a series that quietly proves how powerful a story can be without relying on massive battles, dragons, or world-ending threats. Set in the world of Westeros roughly a century before the events of Game of Thrones, this series takes a different, more intimate approach. Instead of focusing on kings, queens, and grand political schemes, it centers on ordinary people navigating a harsh world shaped by rigid hierarchies, honor codes, and unspoken injustices.

At the heart of the story is Ser Duncan the Tall, known as Dunk, a hedge knight with no famous lineage, no wealth, and no grand destiny-at least not at first glance. Dunk represents a rare perspective in the Game of Thrones universe: a genuinely decent man trying to do the right thing in a society that often punishes kindness and rewards cruelty. His physical size contrasts sharply with his social status; he is literally towering, yet politically insignificant. This contrast becomes a subtle but consistent theme throughout the series, highlighting how power in Westeros has very little to do with virtue.

Alongside Dunk is Egg, a sharp-tongued, intelligent boy whose true identity adds an extra layer of dramatic irony to their journey. Their relationship is the emotional core of the series. It evolves naturally, shaped by shared hardship, mutual dependence, and growing respect. Through their conversations and conflicts, the show explores ideas of mentorship, loyalty, and moral responsibility without ever feeling preachy.

What truly makes A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms stand out is its tone. It feels grounded, almost understated, yet deeply reflective. The series examines knighthood not as a romantic ideal, but as a flawed institution. Honor is questioned, tradition is challenged, and the gap between what knights are supposed to represent and how they actually behave is constantly exposed. In this way, the show feels more philosophical than its predecessors, asking viewers to reconsider what heroism really means.

Visually and narratively, the series embraces restraint. Smaller settings, quieter moments, and personal conflicts replace spectacle, allowing character development to take center stage. This makes the world feel lived-in and real, reminding us that history is not only shaped by great wars, but also by small choices made by imperfect people.

In the end, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms succeeds because it understands that greatness doesn't always come from scale. Sometimes, the most compelling stories are about two travelers on the road, trying to stay true to themselves in a world that constantly pushes them to compromise. That is what makes this show not just good-but genuinely great.

avis:
Familiar World, New Perspectives - *A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms* works because it refuses to feel like a continuation of *Game of Thrones*. Same world, same history, but a completely different lens. Where that series kept widening its scope, this one narrows it. It trades scale for perspective, and more importantly, it shifts its focus away from the powerful and toward the people who usually exist around them.

This is a version of Westeros built around the smallfolk. Not as background texture, but as the environment the story actually lives in. Inns, roads, minor tourneys, passing conversations-these are the settings that matter. Power still exists, but it's distant, filtered through rumor, reputation, and consequence rather than constant proximity.

That shift changes how everything feels. In *Game of Thrones*, decisions reshape kingdoms. Here, they reshape how someone is treated at the next stop, whether they're trusted, whether they eat. The stakes are smaller on paper, but more immediate in practice.

The tone reflects that. It's lighter, more patient, occasionally dry in a way that feels pulled directly from the page. It doesn't ignore the harshness of the world-it just doesn't center it. Instead, it focuses on how ordinary people navigate it, and how close they are to forces they don't control.

There are quiet nods throughout-names, sigils, bits of history-that sit naturally in the background. Nothing is framed like a reveal. It's all just part of the world.

The writing stays out of its own way. Dialogue is simple, often indirect, and rarely explains more than necessary. Conversations circle around meaning instead of stating it outright, which gives scenes room to breathe.

It also captures that specific tone from the source material: sincerity mixed with quiet humor and a constant awareness that reputation and reality rarely align. The show leans into that without emphasizing it, which keeps everything grounded.

The central dynamic is where everything settles in. Peter Claffey's Dunk has the physical presence you expect, but the performance is more restrained than that suggests. There's hesitation there, and a kind of awareness that he's slightly out of place in the role he's trying to fill.

Their relationship builds without being pushed. It feels uneven in a believable way-idealism meeting experience, both adjusting slightly as they go.

Finn Bennett as Aerion Targaryen stands out for a different reason. The performance walks a narrow line between instability and control, and it holds that balance long enough for the character's final moment to feel earned rather than sudden. It doesn't play as spectacle-it plays as inevitability.

The music plays a structural role. It shapes scenes as much as it supports them, reinforcing that reflective, slightly off-center tone the show maintains. It's one of the main elements that helps the series feel consistent with the atmosphere of the original material rather than just its plot.

Visually, the show stays disciplined. It doesn't rely on scale to create impact. It builds scenes around presence-where characters are, how they exist in those spaces, and how those spaces reflect their position in the world.

The show avoids spectacle unless it's necessary. It avoids over-explaining its world. It avoids constantly pulling the story back toward power centers just to remind you they exist.

That last choice is what gives the focus on the smallfolk its weight. The world of kings and councils is still there, but it's not the point. The show trusts that it doesn't need to center it to make it felt.

The pacing reflects this approach-deliberate, sometimes slow, but always controlled. Scenes are allowed to exist without being pushed toward something larger.

This is a series built on precision. It understands the world it comes from, but chooses to move through it at ground level. By focusing on smaller lives and smaller decisions, it ends up revealing parts of that world that larger stories tend to overlook.

It doesn't try to compete with *Game of Thrones*. It shifts the perspective entirely, and in doing so, finds something more specific-and, in a lot of ways, more complete.

Review of S1 - Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is well cast, well filmed, well acted, and has an overall good folktale about a lunkhead with a big heart in a cruel world who earns the high regard of the last decent aspect of the ever-corrupt Targaryen Dynasty. It's a solid addition to the marvelous Game of Thrones universe, and sheds some insight into the age when Targaryen's ruled but the dragons were no gone. It's not a tale of blood and fire or palace intrigue, it's a simple story about a friendship between a Knight and his squire (who just so happens to be an heir to the throne).

However, and there is a however...it's also very short (each episode about 30 minutes) and as a result we get some insight into the life the good knight such as his backstory and why he is the way he is but we learn almost nothing about the rest of the characters and in particular we learn next to nothing about the prince, why he wants to escape his life of conformity in the Targaryen system, and most importantly...we learn and see almost nothing of the knight and the prince learning to trust one another and build a relationship.

There are some tender moments in this show between them, but it's few and far between and way too short, and as a result...when the show ends - I felt it was well meaning and well done but also somewhat empty in its delivery because, quite frankly, it just failed to work the core conflict of the story throughout. And it's just weird, because all the show needed was 10-12 minutes per episode to deep dive into the prince and maybe a few more scenes with he and the knight.

Anyhow, the show has a terrific battle scene in the second to last episode, and we get to meet a ton of interesting (but all too shortly delved into) characters. When it's done I defiantly want to watch another season, but I have to be honest this show was good - and huge kudos to all the actors - but the character development should have been stronger.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms - "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" by George R. R. Martin feels personal in a way the larger A Song of Ice and Fire novels sometimes don't. It's smaller in scale, but bigger in heart. Instead of kings fighting for thrones, we follow one tall, awkward knight and a sharp, stubborn boy trying to find their place in the world.

Dunk isn't perfect. He doubts himself, makes mistakes, and often feels out of his depth - and that's exactly why he feels real. His desire to be a "true knight" isn't about glory; it's about doing the right thing, even when it's hard. Egg, on the other hand, is clever and proud, yet still just a kid learning about the harsh realities of life.

Their journey feels human - full of small choices, quiet bravery, and moments of kindness in a rough world. There's less spectacle, fewer shocking deaths, and more emotional honesty. It reminds you that heroism isn't always loud. Sometimes it's simply choosing honor when no one is watching.

It's warm, thoughtful, and quietly powerful.

The story of a brave knight, based on George R. R. Martin's fantasy world of Westeros, the same setting as Game of Thrones. - The series essentially revolves around a penniless knight who longs to participate in a glorious tournament, accompanied by a young squire who tries to help him in his battles against other characters, both good and bad. It is based on George R. R. Martin's novella, *The Hedge Knight*, the first in a series of three novellas collectively known as the Tales of Dunk and Egg. The "Dunk" in Martin's original text, of course, refers to Duncan, the burly adult squire (former rugby player Peter Claffey) of Ser Arlan of Pennytree (Danny Webb), an outrageously famous hedge knight: this is Martin's term for a knight-errant, a wandering warrior without a lord, title, or fixed lands. Ser Arlan's death leaves Duncan with almost no money, little more than a few horses and a sword. After burying Ser Arlan in the opening scene, Dunk needs more money, reputation, and a squire of his own. He decides to enter a tournament in pursuit of the first two. Dunk finds his second son in Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), a bald stable boy he meets at the most depressing and gloomy roadside inn imaginable. Egg's fearless insolence belies his small stature, a comical contrast to his master's burly physique, and perhaps also to his seemingly humble origins. A fantastic tale that became a legend!

The first two television series, adapted from George R. R. Martin's "A Song of Ice and Fire" saga, tackled epic struggles for the fate of Westeros: civil wars in which an entire fictional continent is plunged into widespread, extensive, and multifaceted chaos, complete with dragons. This series is somewhat undervalued because it features a cast largely unknown to the general public, unlike the previous series, which boasted a large and popular main and supporting cast, more or less familiar to viewers. Set a century before Game of Thrones, it stars Ser Duncan the Tall and his squire, Egg, who wander Westeros while the Targaryen dynasty rules the Iron Throne and dragons are still remembered. Great destinies and enemies await these unlikely friends. The second Game of Thrones spin-off differs in its aims, settings, and perspectives from the original series, offering a gentler, lighter, and mildly humorous take, though still centered on the same violently bloody universe. This third spin-off, "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms," represents a dramatic shift in scale, depicting a typical medieval setting with knights on their gleaming horses clashing in spectacular tournaments, lances at the ready. The complete first season consists of just six episodes, all under 40 minutes long, and a second season is almost certain to follow. The action follows the storyline of a single tournament over the course of just a few days. Unlike the enormous cast that made Martin's novels famous and, later, "Game of Thrones", there is only one character from whose point of view all the action revolves: Ser Duncan the Tall (a childhood nickname that stuck with him), a young wandering warrior on a mission to prove his worth, who will soon be joined by a pleasant and rebellious little bald boy, who will become his inevitable squire, despite the enormous size disproportion, and near the end of the first season his mysterious origins will be revealed in a surprising twist.

The series is quite entertaining, but clearly inferior to the two original series, which are considerably better. Adapted from Martin's novellas "Dunk and Egg," under the supervision of co-creator and showrunner Ira Parker "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" results to be lighter, simpler, and less brutal than "Game of Thrones" or "House of the Dragon," this prequel compensates for its lack of courtly intrigue with exceptional attention to period detail in the fictional era in which it is set, and some genuinely welcome humor. And of course, there are the two endearing protagonists who provide the necessary chemistry and are hard not to like, along with some genuinely funny situations. This is not to prematurely declare the HBO series the creative equivalent of the magnificent Game of Thrones, but rather to underscore both projects' shared interest in the ordinary people, environments, and eras in which they are set, filling in the gaps between the major turning points of their invented worlds. The series familiarizes fans with the lesser-known corners of George R. R. Martin's intricate story, while also offering a more regular, slice-of-life, and atmospheric dose than the main series. "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" takes place roughly 90 years before the events of "Game of Thrones," in a time of relative peace, although, as more than one character points out, the realm is never entirely free of violence, bloodshed, and pain. It's an opportunity to show how Westeros functions when it's not being torn apart and to introduce characters who are not yet involved in its high-level machinations.

Poor Dunk. A gentle giant. Worthy of knighthood next to any of them. - The show has heart. Clichéd line, but you do sympathize with the main character. An orphaned street kid raised under a recluse knight who was a bit unhinged and whose only contact with people involved drinking, whoring, and killing. When his guardian suddenly dies, the kid, now grown and knowing little beyond sleeping under trees and drifting from one town to another with a crazy person, knights himself and sets on his own path to the nearest town and ends up stumbling upon an unlikely friend. I loved the twist midway. I should've seen it coming, but I didn't. Had to rewatch the stable scene in the first episode to realize what I'd missed. The script for both characters is written well. Overall, the writing is inconsistent, but it works. By the end of the fifth season I was like, heck yeah. Game of Thrones is back. At its best, it rivals the OG show, but there are times when it tests your patience.

The biggest problem is that it lacks tonal consistency. It's at its best when it's a serious drama and not a cheap comedy, as there is nothing comedic in the lives of the characters we follow. It's set in a nightmarish world where a teenage girl's throat is cut on screen, where a guy's head is bashed in and all the brain goo spills out in just the goriest manner. Such grotesque events are a daily occurrence in the life of anyone in Westeros. The story unfolds in one of the ugliest fictional worlds imaginable, revolving around mostly tragic affairs, yet literal poo and fart humor are all around. Imagine Prince Oberyn, after taking down The Mountain, emotionally ranting about the atrocities done to his sister and demanding a confession on who ordered him to carry out the horrors, only for Tywin Lannister to let out a loud fart mid-scene, ruining the intense momentum built. Wouldn't that be trash television? Definitely. Cut the crap humor, please.

Also, our protagonist can't be half Hodor and half Jon Snow at the same time. Dunk is supposed to be a complex, endearing, and tragic character, not a bumbling nitwit who bangs his head on doors and stumbles around looking for the exit. Every time the show reduces him to slapstick, it wastes the character. Enough with the stupid humor.

Overall, it's an engaging and entertaining show with great characters, even if it tests your patience at times. I look forward to the upcoming season because the story holds much, much potential.

Every choice shapes the realm and every knight carries the weight of it - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms takes viewers deep into Westeros' quiet, uncertain years. Decades before the events of Game of Thrones. What begins as a tale of political maneuvering and courtly duty evolves into a layered, atmospheric exploration of knighthood, loyalty, and the personal cost of heroism. It's slower, more reflective, and surprisingly intimate. Proof that the world of Westeros has stories beyond dragons and war.

.

Overview (No Spoilers)

Set approximately a century before Robert's Rebellion, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms follows Ser Duncan the Tall (Duncan Targaryen's namesake in legend) and his squire Egg. Together, they journey across Westeros, navigating dangerous politics, forgotten ruins, and morally complex dilemmas that shape the kingdom's future.

The series trades the high-octane battles and intrigue of King's Landing for intimate storytelling: taverns, remote castles, and rural landscapes, where every choice can ripple into history. It's a Westeros that feels quieter, more human, and infinitely richer.

.

✅What Worked

1. Historical Depth and Character Focus: Ser Duncan and Egg are brought to life with nuance, showing that heroism is as much about wisdom and restraint as it is about skill.

2. Westeros as a Living World: From crumbling keeps to village life, the series highlights culture, politics, and everyday survival in vivid detail.

3. Mentorship and Friendship: The bond between Duncan and Egg is touching, adding heart to a story often dominated by war and betrayal.

4. Visual and Cinematic Craft: Wide landscapes, rustic castles, and muted color palettes evoke a medieval realism that's both epic and intimate.

5. Themes of Honor and Moral Complexity: Choices are rarely black-and-white, giving each episode philosophical weight.

6. Quiet Heroism: Unlike other Westerosi tales, the show emphasizes integrity, loyalty, and courage without relying solely on spectacle.

7. Strong Supporting Cast: Lords, ladies, and commoners alike are given depth, making the world feel alive.

.

❌What Fell Short

1. Slower Pacing: The reflective, episodic nature may feel slow to viewers expecting nonstop action.

2. Predictable Political Twists: Some betrayals and courtly maneuvers follow familiar tropes.

3. Limited High Fantasy Spectacle: Dragons and magic are absent, which may disappoint fans of more fantastical entries.

4. Undercooked Minor Antagonists: Some threats feel less threatening compared to the iconic villains of Game of Thrones.

5. Fragmented Storylines: Multiple plot threads occasionally distract from the central journey.

6. Focus on Honor Over Drama: Tension is often moral or emotional rather than explosive.

7. Early Episodes Require Patience: The slow setup may challenge casual viewers.

.

Favorite Moments and Quotes

1. Duncan's quiet reflection on knighthood: "A sword is heavy, but honor weighs heavier."

2. Egg negotiating with a lord who underestimates him, showing his cleverness.

3. Scenes in abandoned castles, where history and decay underscore the impermanence of power.

4. Duncan teaching Egg that courage isn't just fighting, but choosing the right path.

.

If You Liked This, You Might Also Enjoy

1. Game of Thrones prequels for more Westerosi history

2. The Last Kingdom (2015-2022) for nuanced medieval politics and personal honor

3. Kingdom of Heaven (2005) for reflective knightly journeys

4. The Witcher (2019-) for intricate fantasy world-building and character depth

5. Marco Polo (2014-2016) for political intrigue and mentorship arcs

6. The Pillars of the Earth (2010) for historical atmosphere and moral complexity

7. Robin Hood (BBC, 2006-2009) for character-driven heroism

.

Final Thought

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms proves that Westeros is more than dragons, war, and betrayal. It's about the men and women who quietly shape history through honor, loyalty, and courage. Slower, reflective, and deeply human, it's a story of mentorship, morality, and the weight of legacy.

⭐ 8.4/10. A thoughtful, intimate prequel that emphasizes courage, loyalty, and the weight of choices.

We are back in Westeros. - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (2026-) is the third television series in George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire franchise and an adaptation of the Tales of Dunk and Egg series of novellas that was created by Ira Parker and Martin. This series takes places a century before Game of Thrones, where we see Ser Duncan the Tall, and his squire, Egg, wandering through Westeros while the Targaryen dynasty ruled the Iron Throne and dragons were still remembered. As from as my fandom with the franchise,nI binged Game of Thrones (2011-2019) back in 2021 and I absolutely love the show even the final season which gets a lot of hate, but it was actually pretty decent and I have enjoyed House of the Dragon (2022-) thus far. With that being said, I was naturally super excited for this new series and thankfully it didn't disappoint me at all.

Positives for A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (2026-): First off, it felt so good to be back in Westeros in the past with a new cast of characters who are dealing with their own stuff and getting into wild adventures of their own for 6 episodes. Now, I was initially worried about the amount of episodes and the short runtimes at first, but thankfully there is amount story for each episode that give everyone great character development for 30 minutes. As far as the characters go, I really enjoyed Peter Claffey as Ser Duncan "Dunk" the Tall and Dexter Sol Ansell as Prince Aegon "Egg" Targaryen, who are the leads and they are now amongst my favorite characters in Westeros due to their good natured friendship. They are also among the more likable characters I've seen as opposed to the characters from House of the Dragon (2022-) and I love those characters as well, but it was nice to see characters you can actually root for. There is some great banter with every character which is always the case in the world of Westeros that have good bits of humor in them. You still get some of the brutal nature with the action sequences and that made me happy because I love the graphic violences in Westeros. And finally, the Season 1 finale was a nice close to the stories for our characters and it sets up things for Season 2 perfectly.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (2026-) was a nice breathe of fresh air in Westeros and I'm excited for Season 2 to come out next year as well as House of the Dragon Season 3 later this year. If you're a massive Game of Thrones fan like me, then you need to binge this series immediately.

avis:
Six Episodes. Two Episodes of Story - At roughly 30 minutes per episode, this six-episode season amounts to about three hours of storytelling - and even that feels stretched.

This entire arc could have been told in two focused, disciplined episodes.

Instead, we get extended dialogue without escalation. Conversations about politics, honor, succession - but very little narrative propulsion. Characters talk around conflict rather than driving into it. Scenes linger without deepening stakes. The tension never compounds.

The fight between Dunk and the prince doesn't feel inevitable - it feels arranged. Conflict should grow from character flaws colliding under pressure. Here, it feels like the story needed something dramatic to happen, so it simply did.

Slow pacing is not the same as depth. Restraint is powerful when there is subtext boiling underneath. Here, the silence often feels empty rather than loaded.

By the end of the season, there's a lingering sense that there wasn't enough story to justify six episodes. It feels less like a carefully paced drama and more like material stretched to fill a format.

When a season ends and the strongest thought is "that could have been two episodes," something fundamental in structure has failed.

2/10.

avis:
A Humble Tale That Wins the Realm - It was a great watch and an instant favorite for me. It feels refreshingly different from Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon. The tone is lighter, more grounded, and often even humorous, episodes are even shorter. That shift makes perfect sense, we're no longer following the power struggles of great houses, but the journey of a simple hedge knight trying to find his place in the world.

There's something charming and approachable about this perspective. The story feels more personal, sometimes almost prosaic, but in a way that's completely understandable and deeply likable. It doesn't rely on shocking twists or massive battles to keep you engaged. Instead, it takes its time.

And that's one of its greatest strengths: it doesn't rush. The first season allows the story to develop fully and in detail, something many fans wished had happened in the final seasons of Game of Thrones. The slower pace is deliberate, carefully building characters and stakes. And it truly pays off. The final chapters of the season are amazing and genuinely thrilling, delivering emotional weight and tension that feel fully earned because of the patient storytelling that came before.

This is a very welcome addition to the Game of Thrones universe, proof that not every story in Westeros needs dragons and thrones to be compelling. Highly recommended.

avis:
Wholesome - If A Song of Ice and Fire is a grand, sweeping symphony of war and politics, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a beautiful, intimate folk song played by a campfire. This collection of three novellas (The Hedge Knight, The Sworn Sword, and The Mystery Knight) is, without exaggeration, George R. R. Martin's most heartwarming and purely enjoyable work.

Set a century before Game of Thrones, the stories follow Ser Duncan the Tall ("Dunk"), a towering, naive, but honorable hedge knight, and his diminutive, sharp-tongued squire, "Egg"-who happens to be the future King Aegon V Targaryen in disguise. This central dynamic is the book's beating heart. Their relationship evolves from a reluctant partnership to a profound bond of loyalty and brotherhood that rivals any duo in fantasy literature.

What makes this episode a 10-star masterpiece is its perspective. We aren't looking down from the Iron Throne; we are in the mud with the smallfolk. Through Dunk's eyes, we see a Westeros that is still dangerous, but also filled with chivalry, tourneys, and the dusty roads of adventure. The stakes feel smaller than the War of the Five Kings, yet they matter more because we care so deeply about the people involved.

Martin's prose is crisp and immersive, perfectly complemented by Gary Gianni's stunning intricate illustrations (in the illustrated edition), which capture the grittiness and glory of the era.

This is a story about what it truly means to be a knight-not just wearing the armor, but protecting the weak and standing for the truth. It is essential reading for any fan, and frankly, it is simply perfect storytelling.

What we want is the original GOT format with a new story and new characters, lots of them. Complex, layered, jumping from story to story and tying them together. Good writing and unexpected twists. Not a comedic boring drawn out single story. There's an old saying, I don't need to see the labor, show me the baby. I think it applies here. HBO please stop trying to please critics or make something different, just give us what we want. I am hoping it gets better and will probably watch it. A movie split into pieces - I am making this review after the last episode of Season 1 aired(only season so far). This will be free of any spoiler. I am simply stating that this is a review of the complete season.

Now while the tone is purposely very different than Game of Thrones (or House of the Dragon), it happens in the same universe and you should notice the references and easter eggs if you are fan of the previous shows.

That said, it is a story that is "self contained" and appear to be on a smaller scale in a way at first glance, yet does have its consequences in a bigger world.

Personally i enjoyed it for what it was. I am always welcoming more Game of Thrones lore. That said i had one "issue" with it and it is that its basically a movie that they fragmentated into 6 parts.

The episodes are extremely shorts, often at about 30 minutes or so. And if you join them together you can clearly see the structure of a movie with 3 acts, a climax, an epilogue etc. A longer than usual movie you could say? A bit yes, but still a movie.

While not a lot could be considered "padding", you could still trim about 30 minutes and have a runtime of around 2 and a half hours.

Sitcoms are fine for 25-30 minutes episodes, as their purpose is often to make you laugh and have a running gag for the duration of the episode. Also episodes often are "self contained". But when i sit down for "epic fantasy", i like to be a little more immersed for longer times. Some episodes in "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" felt simply like an introduction to the next episode. At 1 per week, it could be a bit "frustrating".

I think this is clearly a "show" that will be more enjoyable being binge watched in 1 go in an evening now that all episodes are available.

Both characters are well-written and there's a great dynamic between them. The show leans more towards the comedy theme, that we haven't seen in any Westeros adaptation, however it worked very well. The stakes never diminishes, however it doesn't allow room for warmth and wit.

The tourney games in Ep 4 & 5 gives an intense view of the world in reality and the harsh truth of power and vulnerability. Episode 5 was a great watch, the action-scenes and the backstory of Ser Duncan was skillfully written.

The show is very bingeable, with only 6 episodes of around 30-35 mins each and I still wonder why there were no more episodes in Season 1. The brotherly chemistry works well, the set-up of their story is solid and there's more we will see from this duo in upcoming seasons.

My Rating : 4/5.

avis:
"A Charming but Too-Safe Journey Through Westeros - A 5/10 Review of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" - Going into A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, I was honestly hyped. A smaller-scale story set in the world of Game of Thrones? Focused on character, not dragons nuking cities every ten minutes? That sounded like exactly the reset the franchise needed after the chaos of House of the Dragon. And... well. It's fine. Just fine. Very aggressively fine.

The biggest strength of the show is its tone. It's quieter, more grounded, and way more human than its predecessors. The relationship between Ser Duncan the Tall and Egg carries the emotional core, and when the series slows down and just lets them talk, it actually works. There's a charm here that feels closer to classic fantasy road stories than to the brutal political chess matches we're used to in Westeros.

But here's the thing: charm alone isn't enough.

For a series based on the novellas by George R. R. Martin, the pacing is strangely uneven. Some episodes drag like they're scared to move the plot forward, while others rush through major moments that should've had more weight. The tournament sequences look decent, but they rarely feel as tense as they should. You keep waiting for that gut-punch moment that defines this universe-and it just... never really lands.

Visually, it's solid but not spectacular. The production design is detailed, and the costumes are great, but it doesn't feel as epic or cinematic as the franchise's earlier entries. It almost feels like the show is trying to prove it doesn't need spectacle-only to end up feeling smaller rather than more intimate.

The writing is hit-or-miss. Some dialogue scenes are genuinely sharp and heartfelt. Others feel oddly sanitized, like the show is afraid to lean into the moral ambiguity that made Westeros iconic in the first place. The political tension exists, but it's dialed down so much that it rarely feels dangerous.

To be clear: it's not bad. There's nothing offensively terrible here. The performances are solid, the world-building is consistent, and longtime fans will appreciate the deeper Targaryen-era lore. But it never reaches the emotional intensity, narrative boldness, or sheer unpredictability that made the franchise legendary.

In the end, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms feels like comfort food in a universe known for breaking your heart. Sometimes that's nice. But if you came in expecting another cultural earthquake? This isn't it.

Final Rating: 5/10 Watchable, occasionally charming, but ultimately too safe to be unforgettable.

avis:
A Different POV on Westeros - AKOTSK is the latest adaptation of George R. R. Martin's works. It distinguishes itself from its predecessors with its much lighter atmosphere, humor, and jovial characters guided by honor and good intentions. We are indeed far from the heavy and sinister Shakespearean tragedies of HOTD and GOT.

Here, the sense of danger associated with Westeros is replaced by a tale of bravery and heroism, where a young hedge knight wishes to participate in a tournament to honor the memory of his deceased mentor. In his quest, he will be aided by a young squire, and it is the relationship between these two characters that initially creates the magic of the series. The story is captivating, and the music and sets succeed wonderfully in immersing us in this fantasy world.

According to some, compared to GOT and HOTD, AKOTSK is the best adaptation of the three, or at least definitely superior to HOTD. That's their prerogative, but it's clearly exaggerated! First, the total runtime of the season is barely equivalent to three episodes of GOT/HOTD. It follows a single story that takes place over just a few days and in the same location, with a very limited number of characters. Obviously, this is much easier to adapt than the dozens of complex plots that make up George R. R. Martin's main saga. The writing is decent, but the characters don't have a lot to say, so it's nothing like the intellectual prowess of Tyrion, Tywin, or Petyr Baelish.

As for HOTD, I can understand that the second season disappointed many, myself included, but some of those who criticize it today 'kinda forgot' how they once praised the talent of Paddy Considine as Viserys, Matt Smith as Daemon, and Rhys Ifans as Otto Hightower. Those who are swooning over AKOTSK for its 'powerful emotions' kinda forgot all those classic scenes like a dying Viserys taking place on the throne with the help of his brother, or young Aemond claiming Vhagar, not to mention all those epic moments from GOT such as Baelor, the outcome of the Mountain vs The Viper, or the first time we see the dragons in the last scene of season one. There is not a single moment in AKOTSK that made me feel anything close to that.

I would also argue that the episode In the Name of the Mother ranks among the best in the franchise, but certainly not with the early seasons of GOT, otherwise you have to admit that Dunk would have died at the end of the battle, considering that Ned never recovered from his leg injury. In this sense, the Trial of Seven is more comparable to the nonsense of BOTB and Jon Snow's plot armor, seeing that despite all his injuries, Dunk gets away with only a black eye. (Someone below lists all the hits Dunk takes during the fight; it's very revealing!) So yes, AKOTSK has a different and refreshing approach. It's a cute little story of chivalry, bravery, and honor like they don't make anymore. It's told in a simple way without the oppressive and dramatic aspects of GOT/HOTD, and it's overflowing with good feelings. It's also perfectly understandable that some fans appreciate that the story focuses on a single plot rather than scattering across dozens of more or less successful subplots like the later seasons of GOT. But I'm still going to wait and see a few seasons (and the third season of HOTD) before placing AKOTSK above the other two and deliberating on its place in history.

avis:
It's not the game, It's Westeros - This is not Game of Thrones. This is Westeros, and for at least the first two episodes, it is glorious.

If you are looking for political intrigue, palace conspiracies, debates over military strategy, or mythical creatures roaming the land, you will not find them here. This is Westeros at peace, and for the most part, that is where it will remain. The only dragons are stitched onto banners. The direwolves remain north of the Wall. The Children of the Forest and the giants exist only in stories, and the realm is secure under the rule of the dynasty that created it.

The world is not changing. It is not on the brink of upheaval. That is not what this story is about.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is about a man trying to remain good in that world, which turns out to present its own challenges, different from those faced when the wheel of power spins, offering the ladder of chaos to anyone willing to climb it. When ambition is quiet and history is not being written in blood, morality is no longer a weapon. It is a choice.

The adventures Ser Duncan the Tall and Egg stumble into will not reshape the fate of great houses or alter the course of history. Familiar names and ancient families appear mostly as brief cameos, there to ground the timeline and reward longtime fans rather than drive the plot. Instead, the story introduces us to the minor lords, the hedge knights, and the smallfolk who make up the overwhelming majority of the realm.

In doing so, it expands Westeros in a way that makes it feel lived in and real, something any fan of world-building or Game of Thrones lore should appreciate. And for those less invested in those, what you are really being offered is the Don Quixote of Westeros.

At its heart, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is about remaining good in a world that makes it all too easy to go bad. Dunk is not especially clever. He is not the best fighter. He is not smooth, calculating, or secretly destined to save the world. He is a regular man, raised to believe in a code, who stubbornly continues to live by it.

When the world darkens and tempts him to abandon that code, Egg is there to remind him of who he is, and more importantly, who he wants to be. Duncan's responsibility to teach another what it means to be a true knight, to impart honor, integrity, compassion, and justice to a boy who admires him, prevents the darkness from consuming the light within him.

It is a refreshing story that manages to feel, at the same time, timeless and timely. This series may not be the most exciting or the most complex Westeros has to offer, but if the remaining episodes are as strong as the first two, it will be one of the most beloved.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is an elite addition to the Game of Thrones universe - My wife and I finished the six-episode A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (2026) on MAX. The storyline follows a knight searching for purpose. He meets a young man and reluctantly takes him on as a squire. As the story unfolds, we learn about the troubled knight's past and upbringing while watching him try to carve out a meaningful role within the Seven Kingdoms-but it won't come easy. Fortunately, his squire proves to be far more useful than he ever anticipated.

The series was created by Ira Parker (House of the Dragon) and stars Peter Claffey (Small Things Like These), Dexter Sol Ansell (The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes), Tanzyn Crawford (Tiny Beautiful Things), and Daniel Ings (The Gentlemen).

I adored about 90% of this series. I loved how it simplifies the story within the Game of Thrones universe. The perspective is largely confined to one point of view, focusing on a single character. That's a refreshing change from the sprawling cast of characters and multiple kingdoms in Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon. Centering the narrative on one knight and his encounters within this world felt intimate and grounded-and it really worked.

The writing is strong throughout. The mindset, experience, and outlook of the two main characters are both fascinating and entertaining. The dialogue is clever and quick, and it's impossible not to like Egg. He keeps things grounded and balanced while serving as the emotional glue of the journey. The acting is elite, and the production value is top tier-easily on par with any prestige historical fantasy series. The attire, props, and settings fully immerse you in the world. The action scenes-especially in Episode 5-are magnificent, with the final battle standing out as a highlight.

The last episode let me down a bit. It felt somewhat slow and slightly disappointing overall, though I did enjoy the final five to ten minutes and the direction it sets up for the next season.

In conclusion, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is an elite addition to the Game of Thrones universe. I'd score it an 8.5-9/10 and highly recommend it.

avis:
A Great Addition to GOT - After Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon, we have a new GOT show in A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms and I have watched all of the 6 episodes, so here is my review for the new show. The premise of the show sees a Hedge Knight, on a quest to truly become a knight when he meets a young squire that will change his life.

Main Character Peter Claffey plays Ser Duncan and he is fantastic in this show. This is the first time I have seen him and he truly encapsulated this role and made me really care about Duncan. He is an interesting character with great development and I really found myself rooting for Duncan, maybe more then any character in this universe.

Supporting Characters Dexter Sol Ansell plays Egg and he is brilliant. He has an extremely bright future and I think this is going to be the start of a great career. Egg is snarky but has plenty of characterisation and the relationship between Duncan & Egg is easily the best part of this show.

Daniel Ings plays Lyonel Baratheon and he provides real energy to this show. Especially over the first few episodes that are a bit slower, he injects life into them and his character is a lot of fun and a real show stealer.

Shaun Thomas plays Raymun Fossoway and he is a great character. He is the ultimate friend for Duncan and he was just a nice character who supported our lead character no matter the circumstances.

Bertie Carvel plays Baelor Targaryen and he is just such a presence on screen. He isn't on the show too much but he owns the show with his presence and is one of the best characters.

Story The story is good, it is much lower stakes then other shows in this franchise but it just works and makes you really care about the characters. The relationship between Duncan and Egg is really well done and the whole concept of the show is really well handled with a pretty satisfying ending.

Script The script is pretty good. It has some really great drama in it that ramps up the issues between some of the characters. There are also some decent humorous scenes which helped Duncan's character. But there is also some humour that really felt out of place and took away from the overall feeling of the show.

Style The style is good, there are some really strong action scenes and it does have the overall feel of Game of Thrones, I just liked the overall vibe of the show. However, the episodes are just too short and to me we could have just got more here and had stronger pacing.

Overall Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a Great show which sets up the stage well for future entries. A few tweaks and it could become just as good as some of the best seasons of Game of Thrones.

Rating - 8/10.

A Breathtaking Masterpiece - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a triumph that brings a fresh, heartwarming, and deeply human perspective to the world of Westeros. By stepping away from the massive scale of dragons and continental wars, the show finds its true power in the small, intimate moments between a hedge knight and his squire.

The series is built on the incredible chemistry between Peter Claffey as Ser Duncan the Tall and Dexter Sol Ansell as Egg. Watching their bond grow from a chance meeting at an inn to a partnership built on genuine respect and honor is the heart of the show. Dunk's simple but unwavering integrity is a breath of fresh air, making him one of the most likable characters in the entire franchise.

Visually, the show is stunning, using natural landscapes and practical sets to create a grounded, immersive version of the Reach. The action, while smaller in scale, carries immense weight because we are so invested in the characters involved. From the colorful chaos of the Ashford tournament to the visceral intensity of the Trial of Seven, every moment feels earned and impactful.

This season is a rare gem that balances the grit of the Game of Thrones world with a sense of hope and adventure. It is a breathtaking 9/10 journey that honors the spirit of George R. R. Martin's novellas perfectly. I am already counting down the days until we get to see Dunk and Egg continue their travels.

Oak and Iron, Guard Me Well - I didn't know much about this series when I started watching it, but I still had high expectations. Partly because it has a very high rating on IMDb, partly because one of the episodes even had a 10/10 rating for a while. And of course, it's a Game of Thrones spinoff. Overall, I thought the series was good, but I expected a bit more.

The story isn't as grand as in Game of Thrones or House of the Dragon. It's a fairly simple story, and that might be why I had a hard time getting into it at first. It's basically about a man who is going to participate in a tournament, and that's pretty much it. It wasn't until around episode four that I really started to like the series. Until then, it felt a bit slow. The characters are good and so is the dialogue, but it's hard to truly connect with them when there are so few episodes and they're relatively short. I also feel like the series lacks a clear villain.

That said, the series is well written and well directed. The action scenes are well choreographed, and the makeup work is very impressive. Episode 5 is the one that previously had a 10/10 rating before some Breaking Bad fans started review-bombing it. While I think it's wrong to review-bomb an episode just because you want Breaking Bad to be the only show with a 10/10 episode, I also don't think episode 5 quite reaches that level. Personally, I would give it a 9/10. For it to reach a full 10/10, I think the episode would have needed a longer runtime, or the series in general could have benefited from longer episodes to build up the story and characters more. That said, it's still a very strong episode where we learn more about Dunk's upbringing and background. The episode's message is about never giving up, which I think is very nice.

Overall, it's a very good first season that has somewhat of an old-school Game of Thrones feel to it. I just wish it had been longer. However, more seasons are on the way, and it's always difficult to review and rate something that isn't finished yet.

I've heard that people who have read the book consider it one of the best adaptations, but I can't really comment on that since I haven't read the book myself. Maybe that's part of the reason why some people think the show is better than I do.

Visually, it maintains the high production value expected from the franchise, though it wisely prioritizes atmosphere over spectacle. The pacing is measured but never dull, giving the characters room to grow.

It may not have the explosive intensity of its predecessors, but its focus and heart make it stand out. A thoughtful, well-crafted addition to the world of cinematic ASOIAF.

Decent but a Bit Meandering - I've heard nothing but good things about Knight of the Seven Kingdoms. Even my favorite YouTube movie critic, The Critical Drinker, raved about it. But boy, I gotta say, I was bored by this show. I binged all 6 episodes last night because I was told it gets better. The pace of the show is glacial and the characters, other than Dunk and Egg, are hardly fleshed out at all. Most are just cardboard cutouts. There is no character arc from episodes 1 to 6. The villains are evil and the heroes are good. No one has any depth. And boy, could this show use some nudity. There is none, except for a very gratuitous scene of the master night urinating. When I say he is hung like a horse, I am not exaggerating. I miss the political intrigue of the original show. The episodes are just over 30 minutes long, but feel like they are 20 minutes, which is odd considering the slow pace. The writers seem to have a very intense infatuation wit bodily functions.

My biggest gripe however is that this is a really poor knockoff of A Knight's Tale. Poor page dons the armor of his deceased master knight, travels to a jousting tournament and picks up compadres along the way while running afoul of the main villain.
