What makes the show work so well is its simplicity: two travelers moving through a dangerous world, discovering honor, loyalty, and harsh reality along the way.

The writing focuses heavily on character development rather than spectacle. There are no dragons or massive battles dominating the story; instead, the series explores the human side of Westeros and the meaning of being a true knight.

Peter Claffey delivers a strong and believable performance as Dunk, portraying a man who is brave, honest, and sometimes naive. Dexter Sol Ansell's Egg adds intelligence and charm, creating a compelling duo that drives the narrative.

Visually, the show still maintains the high production quality expected from this universe. The costumes, armor, music, and cinematography all bring the medieval world to life beautifully.

The pacing can feel slower compared to other shows in the franchise, but that slower pace allows the characters and themes to breathe. By the end, the series proves that Westeros doesn't always need dragons or massive wars to tell a powerful story.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a refreshing addition to the world of Westeros-smaller in scale but rich in character and heart.

avis: Hard-boiled Egg. - 'A Knight Of The Seven Kingdoms (2026)' isn't what I expected from a 'Game Of Thrones (2011-2019)' spin-off and is all the better for it. It's smaller, it's gentler, it's more personal and heartfelt, but it's still just as immersive and detailed and character-driven as its bigger brother. While it's the first tale in Westeros to focus primarily on a single character and to take place over just a few days (in addition to the occasional flashback), it's perhaps more distinct for being about a fundamentally good person. Ser 'Dunk' the Tall is flawed, yes, but he lives by a code of honour and always tries to do what's right, standing in stark contrast to the morally grey - often outright despicable - people who not only surround him but also make up the bulk of the cast of 'GOT'. His relationship with Egg, an enigmatic yet endearingly cheeky chappy who wants to be his squire, is well-observed and really quite moving at times. It's also surprisingly funny, something which can be said for the overall show. This is far more comedic than I expected it to be, and it's also stylistically pretty singular - and sometimes straight-up strange - when compared to its more consistently presented predecessors. It makes some bold choices and it's really invigorating to see a spin-off that doesn't feel as though it's confined by the aesthetics and expectations of its source material. This isn't a referential side dish, it's a delicious main course. The first two episodes are quaint and quite slow, but they're exactly what they need to be. The next three become increasingly compelling and occasionally brutal, making good use of the goodwill garnered by the excellent character work earlier on to keep you bolted to the edge of your seat. The finale is expectedly low-key, as 'GOT' finales usually are, and acts as an enjoyable epilogue that sets up a potential second series perfectly. The season is structured more like a movie, and it isn't much longer than one, but it works well for what it is and certainly doesn't outstay its welcome. I could honestly watch a dozen more seasons - as long as they're a similar quality, of course - and I hope that I at least get to see one or two more. I'm not done with Dunk and Egg just yet, and I don't think anybody else is either. This is a fantastic little show that's sometimes slightly mild precisely because that's what's required of it. It isn't epic, but it's quite immense in its own way. I'd even argue that it's greater than the sum of its parts. I like it a lot.

avis: Lots to like when you can see it. - The sections I could see were very watchable but a great deal was filmed in complete darkness. It might as well have been a radio play. If you are watching this on your TV of a summer's evening then the screen will be a black rectangle with mumbled words coming over your speakers. The words of Egg, in particular, might as well be the chirpings of a canary. On the occasions when the scenes are allowed to be filmed during daylight hours you can see how great it looks. The photography team clearly know what they are doing. This evidence is in short supply during the 'atmospheric' dark scenes when all that can be seen is a glimpse of perhaps one side of a face. For more than half an episode. Generally the show is likeable though and the above complaints are really all about why we have to strain our senses to watch a TV show when the screen is 90 percent black for most of the time. By the way, as usual, the background music is around ten times louder than the dialogue so while you can hear that same tonic chord over and over you might struggle to hear the witty quip written there by the screenplay team. Good luck to them. I like the show but I wish I could watch more of it rather than wonder what is happening in that utter darkness. This of course follows on from House Of Dragons which suffered from the same affliction. A more appropriate title for that might have been: "House Of Talking In The Dark For A Long Time".

avis:
Lots of potential - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms works so well precisely because it doesn't try to outdo the chaos and spectacle that defined so much of Game of Thrones. It's smaller. Quieter. And honestly, that restraint feels intentional - almost confident.

What really carries the series is the relationship between Dunk and Egg. Their chemistry feels lived-in rather than performed, and there's an easy warmth to their dynamic that makes the world feel less brutal and more human. You believe in their bond. It's not just plot-driven partnership - it's mentorship, awkward loyalty, shared uncertainty. That grounding gives the story heart in a way Westeros doesn't always allow itself to have.

The production design deserves credit too. The world feels textured and immersive without screaming for attention. Nothing feels overblown. Instead of dragons dominating the frame, we get dusty roads, quiet conversations, moments of doubt. The storytelling moves deliberately - sometimes almost cautiously - but that patience gives the emotional beats space to land.

What stands out most is the tone. This isn't about kingdoms rising or collapsing under dragonfire. It's about honor. About loyalty. About a young boy learning what kind of king he might become and a hedge knight figuring out what kind of man he already is. That narrower lens actually deepens Westeros. It reminds us that this world isn't only shaped by thrones and wars - it's shaped by the people walking between them.

If there's a critique worth mentioning, it's the episode length. At times, things feel just a little too compact. Not rushed exactly - just... tight. There are moments where you can sense the story wanting to linger a bit longer, to let certain conversations breathe or conflicts unfold more gradually. With material this strong, you almost wish it had the room of a longer arc - maybe even a feature-length format - simply because the character work could absolutely sustain it.

Still, the series ultimately succeeds at what it sets out to do. It tells a grounded, character-driven story in Westeros that feels sincere, focused, and distinct within the franchise. It doesn't rely on spectacle to matter - and that might be its greatest strength.

avis: Best got show - In an era where modern fantasy often prioritizes sprawling geopolitical maps and an ever-increasing body count, George R. R. Martin's A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms serves as a poignant, masterful reminder that the most resonant stories are often the smallest ones told with the most heart. Set roughly a century before the grim winter of A Game of Thrones, this collection of three novellas-The Hedge Knight, The Sworn Sword, and The Mystery Knight-strips away the icy nihilism of the main series to reveal a Westeros that feels sun-drenched, vibrant, and surprisingly earnest. The brilliance of this collection lies in its central duo: Ser Duncan the Tall, a massive, "thick as a castle wall" hedge knight with no true lineage but a desperate, fumbling desire to be honorable, and his squire Egg, a precocious boy whose hidden identity provides a constant, shimmering tension to their dusty travels. Unlike the high lords of the Great Houses who move armies like chess pieces, Dunk and Egg navigate the world at ground level, dealing with the tangible fallout of drought, local feuds, and the lingering scars of the Blackfyre Rebellion. Martin's prose here is leaner and more rhythmic than in his primary cycle, favoring atmospheric detail and sharp, witty dialogue over encyclopedic world-building, which allows the themes of chivalry and class to breathe naturally. We see the Targaryens not as the distant, mad legends they eventually become, but as a family of complex, flawed individuals grappling with the weight of their own dynasty. It is a rare "prequel" that manages to enhance the original material without ever feeling like a chore or a lore-dump; instead, it offers a refreshing, episodic adventure that explores the quiet tragedy of trying to be a good man in a world that primarily rewards the ruthless. By focusing on the bond between a man who has nothing but his shield and a boy who has everything but freedom, Martin crafts a narrative that is both a classic knight-errant tale and a sophisticated deconstruction of the very myths it celebrates, making it an absolutely essential read for anyone who values character depth over sheer spectacle.

When you stick with the source material - After so many disappointing shows that have abandoned their source material A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a breath of fresh air. Ira Parker, the showrunner on AKotSK delivers a spectacular example of what can be when the people creating a show understand the author's vision of the story. The show brings back heroic fiction but with a twist that makes Dunk more human and sympathetic than many main characters in fiction.

The quality of the filming is awesome, especially considering the show budget is not as huge as many contemporary fantasy shows. The world Duncan and his squire Egg inhabit is completely believable giving the show an extremely high immersion factor. The jousting alone may well be the best depiction of jousting ever depicted on film. Likewise, the armor is completely believable and combatants actually wear helmets avoiding the movie silliness of a knight running around in full plate armor with his head totally exposed. Well, except for one brief period.

Bottom line, if you are a book reader or a show only person A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms may well be the best fantasy streaming show ever or at least to this point. Hopefully the following seasons will maintain this spectacular beginning.

avis:
It's a peak show to watch - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a stripped-down, character-driven return to the political world of Westeros-without the dragons, spectacle, or apocalyptic stakes of Game of Thrones or House of the Dragon. Set decades before those events and adapted from George R. R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas, the series focuses on Ser Duncan the Tall and his unlikely squire, Egg. That smaller scope is exactly its strength.

Instead of constant shock value or large-scale war, the show leans into grounded medieval politics, moral ambiguity, and personal honor. Dunk isn't a mastermind or chosen one; he's an underqualified hedge knight trying to do the right thing in a system built on power and lineage. Egg, sharp and observant, quietly represents the future of a broken dynasty. Their dynamic carries the narrative. If their chemistry works, the show works. If it doesn't, nothing else will save it.

The pacing is slower than modern fantasy blockbusters, but that's intentional. The tension builds through tournaments, oaths, reputation, and class conflict rather than dragons burning cities. It feels more intimate and, at times, more realistic. That said, viewers expecting constant action will be disappointed. This isn't spectacle fantasy; it's political and character drama with swords.

Where it has the potential to surpass its predecessors is tone. If executed faithfully, it can capture the moral complexity that early Game of Thrones mastered before it drifted into rushed storytelling. The writing must stay sharp and resist unnecessary expansion or filler.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms has the ingredients to be a thoughtful, tightly written fantasy drama. Its success will depend entirely on disciplined storytelling and strong performances-not scale.

Writers are obsessed with bodily excretions - A lot of what is supposed to be comic relief just comes across as tone-deaf and disrespectful to the viewer. I don't know about you, but the sight of a grown man taking a dump doesn't send me into guffaws. Neither does full frontal nudity of an old man with a large prosthetic dong. You can expect that, and a lot of old men hocking up loogies. Because again, "comedy".

I just about turned this series off for good after getting to see a horse defecate in ep. 3. Part of me wonders if this isn't some kind of meta take the writers are doing. Like, "yea you dumb peasant, you like that? You were looking forward to GOT? Mhmm here you go" (scene of dunk splattering from his loins). "You will take your 30 minute episode filled with poo gags and be grateful for it!!"

If you can get past all of that, the show has some merits. The pacing is good. Dunk is a little hard to root for - "Oh, sir plot device isn't available right now? I 'spose I'll come back on the 'morrow". I get that there's been a big push to deconstruct the typical male hero, and that some of it has to do with the source material, but a lot of these "deconstructed" characters in today's television have become a bit exhausting for me personally.

The music is also a bit goofy, to the point where it can be rather immersion-breaking. I don't remember what was played at the end of episode 3, all I remember is that I cursed out loud in confusion due to it being so out of context.

Also, I'm not a fan of Egg. The way he talks for a 10-yea-old, I just can't buy it.

I'm struggling to find what I liked about the show, since I trudged through it for a bit. But I probably won't be going back. That was one poop too many for me and I feel like its a matter of dignity at this point.

Nothing in it feels earned. The stakes aren't real because the story has already discarded logic, motivation, and consequence. It's a bad version of a series that was already barely holding itself together by the time it reached its final season. Characters you used to care about act inconsistently, humor falls flat, and the slow pacing just reminds you that GoT's supposed depth was mostly smoke and mirrors.

In short: it's Game of Thrones stretched thin - boring, padded, and utterly forgettable.

Dunk is not a typical legendary hero; he is flawed, inexperienced, and sometimes uncertain. This vulnerability makes him relatable and human.

The series also explores themes of honor, class differences, and the true meaning of knighthood. Instead of focusing solely on battles and spectacle, it examines what it means to be good in a world filled with ambition and corruption. The political tension is present but subtle, giving viewers space to connect deeply with the characters.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms promises a more character-focused and thoughtful experience within the larger fantasy universe. It offers a slower pace, emotional depth, and a nostalgic return to the rich world-building that fans love, while carving out its own unique identity.

avis:
A Love Letter to Westeros - I've loved ASOIAF for years, but AKOTSK is the first show where I've felt truly immersed in the world of Westeros.

The simple story, intimate POV, and lighthearted tone give the pacing - and the world - room to breathe. Watching Dunk and Egg crack eggs, cheer at tourneys, and dig in the mud during tug-of-war felt more like having a great time at a Ren Fest than watching a GOT prequel. What truly made GRRM's world feel vivid and alive, though, was the production team's superb craftsmanship. Every detail felt tactile and intentional; at Lyonel's feast, I didn't just think, "That's great lighting" - I felt the warmth of the candlelights and the safety and sense of a home it provided Dunk.

Peter Claffey and Dexter Sol Ansell *are* Dunk and Egg. I felt the bond between Dunk and Egg as part of the show's atmosphere, even when they weren't in scene together. There's an organic affection and loyalty in their performances that makes this show feel so wholesome and precious. Dunk's awkwardness and Egg's sharpness create some of the best moments in the series.

The entire cast was perfectly cast, as well. I was surprisingly moved by Sam Spruell's Maekar; he adds a layer of vulnerability and depth to the prince that I didn't particularly feel in the books or graphic novels, so I'm excited to see more of him in Season 2... especially after that post-credit scene.

As this is a non-spoiler review, all I'll say is that Ep. 4 & 5 are peak storytelling (that fog was its own main character) and a testament to why we still need stories about goodness and heroes, no matter how trite they've become. The power of the show - exemplified in those episodes and much like in knighthood - is in its honesty and care for the little things. No dragons needed.

Altogether, this show feels like the long overdue love letter to GRRM and his world of Westeros. The entire team clearly gave this their all, and it paid off brilliantly. I've been playing it on repeat, excited for more, and will probably continue to do so until the next season airs.

Good knigth - A Breath of Fresh Air in Westeros: Why "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" is a Masterpiece of Restraint For years, the name "Westeros" has been synonymous with grand-scale political intrigue, fire-breathing dragons, and world-ending threats. However, HBO's latest venture, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, proves that the most compelling stories in George R. R. Martin's universe can also be the most intimate. By shifting the focus from the Iron Throne to the dusty roads of the Reach, the series recaptures the heart and soul of the franchise.

At its core, the show is a character study of an unlikely duo: Ser Duncan the Tall (Peter Claffey) and his diminutive squire, Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell). Claffey brings an incredible sense of "noble humility" to Dunk; he is a man who isn't the smartest or the most skilled warrior, but he possesses a moral compass that feels radical in a world defined by cynicism. Opposite him, Ansell's portrayal of Egg is a revelation-balancing a hidden royal heritage with the boisterous curiosity of a child. Their chemistry is the engine that drives the series, making every tavern conversation as gripping as any dragon duel.

Visually, the series is a triumph of "grounded fantasy." Instead of CGI-heavy battles, we are treated to the vibrant pageantry of a medieval tournament at Ashford Meadow. The production design prioritizes historical texture-worn leather, dented armor, and the lived-in mud of a traveling camp-giving the Seven Kingdoms a tangible, gritty reality that feels more immersive than ever.

While some may find the shorter 30-to-40-minute episodes a departure from the usual hour-long HBO epic, this brevity works in the show's favor. It mirrors the focused, episodic nature of the original novellas, ensuring that every scene serves the development of the characters rather than filling a runtime.

Ultimately, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms succeeds because it remembers that chivalry isn't about magic; it's about the choices made when no one is looking. It is a warm, humorous, yet occasionally brutal reminder of why we fell in love with this world in the first place. It is, quite simply, the best adaptation of Martin's work to date.

The story follows Ser Duncan the Tall (Dunk), a humble and honorable hedge knight, and his sharp-witted squire Egg, who is secretly Aegon Targaryen. The world-building remains rich and detailed, but it never overwhelms the reader; instead, it provides historical depth that enhances the lore of Westeros without requiring prior knowledge of the main series. The pacing is steady, the dialogue is sharp, and the themes of honor versus reality are thoughtfully explored. Unlike darker fantasy tales that rely heavily on brutality, this book balances realism with hope, making it both engaging and meaningful. Where Game of Thrones made me impatient for the next episode, this show made me impatient for the episode to end. What should have been a worthy successor instead feels like an expensive experiment in how long an audience will tolerate boredom. It doesn't subvert expectations-it simply fails to meet them.

avis:
It is, quite simply, BRILLIANT! - A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (HBO) HBO's A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is, quite unexpectedly, a triumph of tonal precision. In a television landscape often burdened by excess - excess spectacle, excess solemnity, excess myth-making - this series demonstrates something far rarer: restraint.

Adapted from George R. R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas, the production wisely eschews the operatic scale of Game of Thrones in favor of intimacy. And in doing so, it achieves something arguably more profound. Where Thrones was Shakespearean in its political sprawl, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is Chaucerian - earthy, ironic, deeply human, and acutely aware of the absurdity embedded within systems of power.

The writing is the series' most distinguished asset. It understands that wit need not undercut gravity; rather, it sharpens it. Dialogue carries a wry intelligence reminiscent of medieval romance filtered through modern sensibility. Humor arises organically from character rather than circumstance, and it functions not as relief from violence but as commentary upon it. The world is bloody and gritty - yes - but never gratuitously so. Brutality feels historical rather than performative.

Peter Claffey's Sir Duncan the Tall ("Dunk") anchors the series with remarkable sincerity. His performance resists the temptation toward heroic grandiosity. Instead, he embodies moral bewilderment - a man navigating chivalric ideals in a world that persistently betrays them. There is a quiet vulnerability in his physicality, a sense that Dunk's size is both armor and burden. Claffey allows pauses to breathe; he trusts stillness. In an era of overwrought fantasy acting, this restraint feels almost radical.

Visually, the production design leans toward lived-in realism. Armor is dented. Cloaks are weathered. Mud remains mud. The cinematography favors natural light and grounded composition, reinforcing the narrative's human scale. One senses not a mythic kingdom, but a precarious feudal society held together by fragile codes of honor.

Perhaps most impressive is the show's tonal equilibrium. It is witty without flippancy, serious without self-importance, and violent without indulgence. It captures the paradox at the heart of Martin's universe: that heroism is often accidental, that nobility is flawed, and that power structures are sustained by illusion as much as steel.

In short, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms succeeds because it understands that epic storytelling need not always be epic in scale. Sometimes, the most compelling drama lies not in thrones or dragons, but in the moral education of a single man trying, imperfectly, to do what is right.

It is, quite simply, brilliant.

What stands out most is how the series captures the human side of this fantasy world. Small conversations, moral choices, and simple adventures carry emotional weight, proving that compelling storytelling does not always need massive action sequences. This grounded approach makes the story feel authentic and memorable.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a beautifully crafted series that successfully expands the Westeros universe while offering a fresh perspective. It is charming, heartfelt, and deeply enjoyable - a must-watch for longtime fans as well as newcomers who appreciate strong storytelling and meaningful characters.

Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is one of the best shows I have seen to date and DEFINITELY the best thing I have watched one 2026 and better than ANY of the garbage I watched in 2025.

Visually, it maintains the cinematic quality we expect from HBO, but the real strength lies in tone. It feels grounded. Focused. Mature. There's no rush to shock the audience - only to immerse them.

In fact, this single season delivers more narrative consistency and emotional coherence than at least four seasons of Game of Thrones. It reminds us why we fell in love with this universe in the first place.

If this is the standard going forward, Westeros is in very good hands.

A flawless 10/10.

avis:
Finally, a Westeros Show You Don't Need a PhD to Enjoy - Okay so hear me out. What if a Game of Thrones show was actually... fun? Not fun in a guilty pleasure way, but genuinely warm, well-crafted, and easy to get into? Because that's exactly what A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms pulled off, and I think it deserves way more conversation than it's getting.

Created by Ira Parker and George R. R. Martin, the series is the third entry in the Game of Thrones franchise, premiering on HBO on January 18, 2026, and running for six episodes. It's based on Martin's novella The Tales of Dunk and Egg, and unlike its predecessors, it's not trying to be an epic. That restraint is exactly what makes it work.

What's It About?

The show follows Duncan "Dunk" the Tall (Peter Claffey), an awkward man who desperately wants to become a knight. Alone after the death of his mentor, he decides to enter a tournament as a way to make money and prove himself. Along the way, he ends up with a travel companion: Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), a mysterious bald kid who refuses to leave his side. Egg is resourceful and worldly-wise far beyond his years and doesn't quite share Dunk's bumbling naivety.

The story is set after House of the Dragon and before Game of Thrones, at a time when the Targaryens still hold the Iron Throne but all the dragons are already gone. No white walkers, no massive wars. Just two guys on the road, trying to survive.

What Works and What Doesn't?

The biggest strength here is actually the simplicity. Where Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon were packed with lore, family trees, and political webs you basically needed a wiki to follow, this show requires zero prior knowledge. And that's not a knock on complexity. It's a genuine creative choice that pays off, because it forces the story to earn your attention through character rather than mythology.

Dunk is written as someone who keeps choosing what's right over what's smart, and watching that play out across six episodes gives the show its actual spine. It's not just a "nice guy tries hard" arc. His decisions have real consequences, and the show doesn't let him off the hook for them. That's what separates it from feeling like comfort TV with no stakes.

The chemistry between Claffey and Ansell also carries a lot of weight. Their pairing is what makes the whole show sing, and I'd agree with that. Scenes that could've been slow or expository become genuinely watchable just because of how these two interact.

The show also shifts tone deliberately, with the first half feeling lighter and adventurous before the back half gets noticeably darker. It's a structure that works, though it does mean the early episodes can feel a little too breezy before the story finds its footing.

The clearest weakness? Female characters are largely limited to love interests or sex workers, who end up as plot devices to push Dunk forward rather than fully realized people. For a show that feels fresh in so many other ways, that's a frustrating pattern that's hard to ignore by the third or fourth time it happens.

Who's It For?

This one works well for two very different audiences. If you're already a Game of Thrones fan, it offers a quieter, more grounded corner of a world you know. If you've never watched any of it and always found the franchise too dense or too brutal.

It's not a perfect show, and the writing does let certain characters down. But as a six-episode story about one man trying to do the right thing in a world that rarely rewards it, it lands more often than it misses.

I'll give it a solid 9/10 ⭐

The storytelling is thoughtful and character-driven, allowing relationships and personalities to develop naturally. The slower pace works in the show's favor, creating a sense of intimacy that draws viewers into the journey.

The performances are outstanding throughout. The central characters feel genuine and relatable, and their interactions bring warmth and humanity to a world often defined by hardship. Moments of humor and friendship balance the harsher realities, making the emotional impact even stronger.

Visually, the series is beautifully crafted. Costumes and locations feel authentic and lived-in, and the cinematography captures both the beauty and roughness of the setting. Instead of relying on spectacle, the show focuses on atmosphere and detail, which makes the world feel real and immersive.

Perhaps the greatest strength of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is its consistency. Every episode contributes meaningfully to the overall story, maintaining a steady tone and clear sense of purpose.

Overall, this is a near-perfect fantasy series. It combines strong writing, memorable characters, and rich world-building into a deeply satisfying experience. A must-watch for both longtime fans and newcomers alike.

avis:
No that good - I wanted to love this. I really did. But after sitting through what felt like an eternity disguised as an evening of entertainment, I left feeling cheated, bored, and mildly insulted.

The concept had potential - a sprawling, Game of Thrones-inspired immersive experience promising intrigue, drama, and spectacle across seven distinct "kingdoms." What it delivered instead was seven distinct disappointments, each one somehow worse than the last.

"Ambitious" is a Generous Word The production design looked like it was assembled on a Tuesday afternoon with a budget scraped together from a medieval-themed birthday party. The banners were crooked, the costumes looked suspiciously like rental Halloween fare, and at least two of the "kingdoms" were separated by nothing more than a velvet rope and wishful thinking.

The Performances The cast appeared to be operating under the impression that shouting equals acting. Every lord, every queen, every mysterious hooded figure delivered their lines with the kind of desperate intensity that suggested they were being graded on volume alone. Subtlety was not invited to this kingdom.

The Story Goes Nowhere For an event billing itself as an immersive narrative experience, surprisingly little actually happens. Characters threaten each other endlessly without consequence. Alliances are formed and broken within minutes for no discernible reason. By the third kingdom, I had completely lost track of who wanted what and, more importantly, stopped caring entirely.

The Audience Interaction At one point an actor grabbed my arm and whispered cryptically, "The raven knows your name." I do not know what this meant. Neither, I suspect, did he.

The Verdict A Night of Seven Kingdoms is the kind of event that mistakes busyness for excitement and noise for drama. It is exhausting without being thrilling, complex without being interesting, and long without being epic.

Save your money. Stay home. Rewatch actual Game of Thrones - even the final season is a more satisfying experience than this.

1/5 - and that point is purely for the decent wine selection.

avis:
Best show ever after GOT - Best one yet. I just finished watching Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, and honestly, I didn't expect to love it this much.

Going in, I thought it would just feel like a smaller spin-off set in the world of Game of Thrones - but it turned out to be something much more heartfelt and personal. Instead of massive wars and constant political chaos, this show focuses on two characters: Dunk and Egg. And somehow, that smaller scale makes everything feel more real.

What I loved most was the relationship between them. Dunk isn't a perfect knight - he's rough around the edges, unsure of himself, and constantly trying to live up to an ideal of honor. Watching him struggle with what it truly means to be a knight felt refreshing. Egg, on the other hand, brings intelligence, confidence, and just enough mystery to keep things interesting. Their bond slowly grows in a way that feels natural and earned, not rushed.

Compared to Game of Thrones, this series feels quieter but more emotionally grounded. Game of Thrones was intense - betrayals, shocking deaths, dragons, and large-scale battles. It was epic in every sense. But Knight of the Seven Kingdoms feels more intimate. The stakes are smaller, yet somehow they hit harder because you're deeply invested in the characters rather than the politics of entire kingdoms.

That's not to say the world-building isn't strong. Westeros still feels rich and layered, just like in the universe created by George R. R. Martin. But here, you see it from the ground level - from inns, tournaments, and dusty roads rather than royal courts. It makes the world feel lived-in and human.

Another thing I appreciated was the tone. It still carries the realism and moral complexity that fans expect, but there's a subtle warmth to it. There are moments of humor, quiet reflection, and genuine friendship that Game of Thrones rarely allowed itself.

By the end, I felt strangely attached - not overwhelmed by spectacle, but emotionally satisfied. If Game of Thrones was about power and ambition, Knight of the Seven Kingdoms feels like it's about honor and growth.

I genuinely can't wait for more. It reminded me why I fell in love with this world in the first place - not just for dragons and wars, but for the people living inside it.

Despite being based on promising source material, the series fails to deliver the depth, excitement, and emotional impact that fans expected.

One of the biggest problems is the slow and unfocused storytelling. Many episodes feel unnecessarily long, filled with dull conversations and repetitive scenes that add little to the plot. Instead of building tension, the show often feels like it is wasting time. Important moments are rushed, while unimportant ones are dragged out, making the pacing extremely frustrating.

The characters are another major weakness. While Ser Duncan and Egg had great potential, their development feels shallow and predictable. Their relationship lacks emotional depth, and many side characters are forgettable. Unlike earlier Game of Thrones characters, these people rarely feel complex or realistic.

Visually, the show is decent but far from impressive. The settings and costumes are acceptable, yet they lack the epic scale and richness that made the original series special. Several battle scenes feel cheap and poorly choreographed, reducing their impact.

The dialogue is also disappointing. It tries too hard to sound "medieval" and poetic, but often ends up sounding forced and unnatural. Many conversations feel awkward and unconvincing, breaking immersion.

Worst of all, the series lacks originality. It relies too heavily on nostalgia and references to past shows instead of creating its own identity. Rather than feeling fresh, it feels like a weak imitation of better stories.

Overall, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is a missed opportunity. With weak pacing, flat characters, and uninspired writing, it fails to live up to its potential. Fans expecting another great fantasy series will likely be left disappointed.

It's about how a very simple person, who has nothing but faith in ideals and values but no real chances, relies on his own strength and hope to survive events that seemingly should have ended before they even began. The line between valor and poverty or banditry is honor; every manifestation of it carries immense weight because everything is at stake. This makes the character feel very alive and authentic. avis:
HBO worst Ever - HBO's A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms promised to be a spiritual successor to Game of Thrones, but for many viewers, it has been a frustrating experience. Across three episodes, the series managed to stretch what could have been compelling material into a painfully slow narrative that left audiences feeling cheated out of their time.

The biggest issue lies in the pacing. Each episode drags with long stretches of dialogue that fail to build tension or deepen character arcs. Instead of sharp exchanges or gripping conflicts, the script meanders, often circling back to the same themes without adding new layers. This sluggish storytelling makes the three hours feel like a chore rather than an immersive journey.

Another disappointment is the lack of dramatic stakes. Game of Thrones thrived on unpredictability, shocking betrayals, and morally complex choices. In contrast, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms seems hesitant, almost timid, in its approach. Characters wander through scenes without urgency, and the plot unfolds with little sense of danger or consequence. Viewers expecting intrigue and intensity are left with bland conversations and predictable outcomes.

The script itself feels underdeveloped. Dialogue often comes across as filler, with characters stating the obvious or repeating sentiments already expressed. Instead of sharp wit or memorable lines, the writing leans heavily on exposition, slowing the momentum even further. This lack of narrative punch makes the episodes feel hollow, as though the writers were stretching thin material to meet runtime requirements.

Visually, the production retains HBO's high standards-lavish sets, atmospheric lighting, and strong costume design-but these strengths cannot mask the weakness of the storytelling. A beautiful frame loses its impact when the scene inside it lacks energy or purpose.

Ultimately, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms fails to capture the magic of its predecessor. What should have been a thrilling exploration of Westeros' history instead becomes a tedious slog. For viewers who invested three hours across three episodes, the disappointment is palpable. HBO had the resources and legacy to deliver something extraordinary, but instead, it offered a slow, uninspired script that squandered its potential.

The world-building is also impressive. The stories explore various regions of Westeros, showcasing the **political intrigues** and social structures that fans enjoy. Martin skillfully weaves in historical context and lore, making the stories feel rich and layered.

Some readers may find the stories slower-paced compared to the thrilling drama of "Game of Thrones." The focus is more on character growth and personal quests than on epic battles or grand political schemes.

Overall, "The Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" is a **valuable addition** to Martin's work, appealing to both new readers and longtime fans. The mix of humor, character exploration, and the complexities of Westeros history makes it an engaging read that expands the lore of this beloved universe.

The knight of the seven kingdom - There's something strangely comforting about A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms. After years of watching Westeros implode in betrayal, fire, and political paranoia, this series feels smaller, quieter... and somehow more sincere.

This isn't about dragons reshaping the world. It's about two people walking through it.

Dunk isn't a legendary warrior or a master strategist. He's just a decent man trying to live up to an ideal that the world barely respects anymore. And Egg, sharp and observant, sees more than he lets on. Their relationship is the emotional core of the show. It feels natural, not manufactured. You don't watch them because the plot demands it. You watch because you care.

The beauty of the series is in its restraint. The stakes aren't world-ending, but they feel personal. A tournament matters. A decision matters. A moment of honor matters. And that makes everything land harder.

It reminds you that Westeros isn't just built on kings and queens. It's built on ordinary people navigating a system stacked against them. The show doesn't shout. It doesn't overwhelm you with spectacle. It trusts the characters to carry the weight.

And honestly? That trust pays off.

If Game of Thrones was about power and consequence, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms feels like it's about integrity. About what kind of person you choose to be when nobody's writing songs about you.

It's slower. It's softer. But it sticks with you.

It proves that you don't need a thousand characters to tell an epic story. Whether you are a die-hard fan of the lore or a newcomer, this show is a cinematic triumph that captures the true essence of knighthood.

avis:
Bad - Waited years for a new Game of Thrones story, and this is what HBO gives us? A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is hands-down one of the most boring, misguided spin-offs I've ever seen. Where do I even start?

First off, the tone is all wrong. They turned what should be a grounded, chivalric tale into some kind of slapstick comedy with way too much forced humor. The very first episode opens with Dunk basically sh*tting himself in the woods for "shock value" laughs-really? Potty humor and immature gags every five minutes? This isn't a kids' cartoon; it's supposed to be in the same universe as brutal betrayals and dragonfire. The constant juvenile jokes completely kill any sense of stakes or seriousness. It feels like they're trying to make a medieval buddy comedy instead of a proper ASOIAF adaptation.

The pacing is glacial. Episodes are ridiculously short-some barely hit 30 minutes-and just when something interesting might happen, it cuts off. You're left hanging week after week with barely any payoff. They stretch a simple novella into six episodes, but nothing much actually happens. Dunk wanders around, Egg sasses him, rinse and repeat. No epic battles (the Trial of Seven is a foggy mess you can barely see-budget cuts, really?), no real intrigue, just meandering character "development" that drags on forever.

Dunk himself is a lumbering oaf with zero charisma. Peter Claffey might be trying, but the character comes off as dumb as a bag of hammers-constantly making the worst decisions and somehow still bumbling into "hero" moments. Egg is annoying more than endearing, and their chemistry feels forced rather than natural. The rest of the cast? Forgettable. The Targaryens look like they wandered in from a different show.

Worst of all, they hid key action behind fog and bad lighting choices, repeating the same mistakes from GoT's "The Long Night" and House of the Dragon's dark episodes. I paid for a visual spectacle, not squinting at shadows during what should be the season's big fight scene. It's lazy filmmaking.

If you're expecting dragons, politics, or anything resembling the gripping drama of early Game of Thrones, look elsewhere. This is a lightweight, corny, overly comedic snoozefest that feels like it was made for people who hate what made the original great. HBO clearly doesn't know what to do with Martin's world anymore.

Avoid unless you want to see Westeros turned into a bad sitcom. 1/10.

avis:
Average drama, terrible history - The cast is packed with talent. The cinematography is excellent. The stakes couldn't be higher. In these regards, it's a success as a drama.

The issue is everything else. The script couldn't be more boiler plate. It even has the trope of ending some sentences with "was it not" just to make it sound old timey. This is a cliche that has been used in numerous times in poor historical dramas. The actors are good, but they still have to spit out the lines that they're given and the script isn't as strong as the performances.

Then there is the history. Let's just leave it that despite this being a genuinely exciting time with larger than life characters and a genuine series of epic and exciting events. I have no idea why the writers just decided to make most of it up.

We have Anglo-Saxons wearing tartan, the armour is largely wrong as our most of the architecture. Battle tactics and interactions between key people are nonsense. The question has to be who is this for? If you're a fan of history, get it right. If you can't be bothered to tell the historical story then write a fantasy like the Witcher. This is an example of a project that will keep nobody happy.

I have literally written a book about the complexities of bringing the past to life. If you're interested, it's called- Hollywood and History by Jem Duducu. This is one of these examples where it has a veneer of quality to it but the reality is this is as high fantasy as the movie 300. It's a solid enough drama just don't call it history.

avis:
An uneven recreation of the historical events leading up to the significant Battle of Hastings in 1066. - Series dealing with the familiar story of a deadly confrontation that would define the future of a country-and a continent-for a thousand years. William of Normandy, ¨The Conqueror¨(Nikolaj Coster-Waldau) and Harold of Wessex (James Norton)were destined to meet at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. They were allies but had no claim to the British monarchy, and fate pitted them against each other for the country's crown.

The series is a historical epic that, despite its stellar cast, doesn't feel particularly historical or epic, so much so that it lacks the necessary spectacle and instead denotes a somewhat meager setting and limited budget. This series doesn't accurately depict what happened in or before the Battle of 1066. It attempts to explain why it happened, but gets caught up in court intrigue and family problems that don't entirely please the average viewer, who is looking for more clarity, not too complex and lightness in the historical facts. So that in its eagerness for ahistorical detail, it becomes a frustrating experience to watch.

Interpretations of a decent cast are pretty good, most of them performing historical roles, such as: James Norton as Harold Godwinson, Nikolaj Coster-Waldau as William the Conqueror, Clémence Poésy as queen Matilda creator of the famous Bayeauux Tapestry, Emily Beecham as Edith, Eddie Marsan as king Edward the Confessor , his mother Lady Emma played by Juliet Stevenson, and Jean-Marc Barr as King Henry of France. And there is a not-too-spectacular recreation of famous battles, such as: The Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25th September 1066 that marked the end of the Viking era in England, as Harald Hardrada's invasion was the last major Viking attempt to conquer the country; and on 14th October 1066, just 19 days later, the Battle of Hastings took place. This TV miniseries in 8 episodes, created by Michael Robert Johnson, was professionally directed by Erik Leijonborg, Bálint Szentgyörgyi, Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, Baltasar Kormákur, but nothing special.

Adding more historical data to that already presented in the series: A descendant of Vikings, William the Conqueror was Duke of Normandy from 1035 under the name of William II. After a long struggle to consolidate his power, by 1060 his hold on Normandy was consolidated, and he began planning the conquest of England, which began in 1066. The rest of his life was marked by incessant struggles to maintain his possessions, both in England and northern France, and by the difficulties and disagreements with his eldest son, Robert Courteheuse. William was the son of Robert I, Duke of Normandy, and his concubine Arlette de Falaise. His status as an illegitimate son and his youth caused him numerous difficulties when he succeeded his father, as did the anarchy that spread throughout his domains in the early years of his duchy. During his childhood and adolescence, the Norman nobles fought among themselves both to control the young duke and for their own benefit. In 1047, William suppressed a rebellion and began to consolidate his power over the duchy, a process that did not culminate until 1060. In the 1050s, he married Matilda of Flanders, gaining a powerful ally in the neighboring County of Flanders. During this same period, William appointed several of his supporters as bishops and abbots of the Norman church. This consolidation of power allowed him to expand his horizons, and in 1062, he secured the neighboring province of Maine. From the 1050s, William was a pretender to the throne of England, then held by his cousin Edward the Confessor, who had no children. However, he was not the only one who coveted the English crown, as he had a powerful rival, the Anglo-Saxon earl Harold Godwinson, who was named his successor by King Edward himself on his deathbed in January 1066. William argued that the King of England had previously promised him that the throne would be his and that Harold himself had sworn to support him. Therefore, the Norman duke launched a military intervention and prepared a large fleet and a powerful army that landed in southern England in September 1066 and defeated Harold's forces at the Battle of Hastings on October 14. William also defeated Harold's successor in office, Edgar Atheling, who was de facto King of England for just over 70 days before surrendering to William's forces. Thus, William forged a direct path to the English throne and was crowned King of England in London on Christmas Day 1066.

avis:
Missed opportunity - There is a distinct lack of material within tv or cinema based around late Anglo Saxon England, specially the and of Anglo Saxon England. There have been a good few straight to DVD movies over the last 15-20 years which on the whole have all been garbage. The BBC's King and Conqueror series offered a real chance to do it right. Sadly it has not.

There will be people who aren't so historically minded that will enjoy this series as a period, sword and shield, kings and queens type show but the reality is it's just not been done well. Even taking out the constant liberties it takes with the real history the script, costume and acting are on the whole just bad. At times the acting feels wooden, forced and not believable. The writing again at times, not always, lacks imagination and is plain boring. There are no moments that cause you to take any real notice of the show.

The racially diverse cast does also take away from the ability of a show like this to immerse you in the period. When you watch a period piece you want to feel like you are watching that time period. There are some shows from the last 20 years that do this, HBO Rome, the earlier seasons of the Last Kingdom, even The Tudors all all its historical liberties. These shows actually make you feel like you could be watching the period it's trying to recreate. But King and Conqueror, with a black Earl of Mercia and a black Thane Thomas, it detracts from the ability of the show to pull you into the time period. Whilst I do not doubt there were black people present in Anglo Saxon England they would have been extremely rare and in some parts of the country almost a myth. I do not take away from the skill of Jason Forbes and Elander Moore who on the whole act well along with Nikolaj Custer-Waldau but again just make it at least a true reflection of society at the time.

It is a shame that this show was not done better. I've anticipated it for the last year and it's fallen flat in my opinion. Edward the Confessor was also portrayed as a weak puppet. I don't doubt he was a very pious and indecisive man but there is evidence he enjoyed hunting and other more manly, kingly pursuits of the time. I would not feel the need to go back and rewatch/enjoy this series again.

King & Conqueror was very entertaining when you look at it with an open mind trying to tell a story to a newer generation. I believe that every story told on the screen is an invitation for others to open their history books and read what actually happened. There are a lot of holes in history itself, even in the context of this story. But this was very well made without taking it into three separate seasons, which I believe it might have taken to tell this entirety of this story.

If someone wants to see what actually happened in history, go watch a documentary or dare I say read a book written about that time and what the people went through. I will not bash any movie that has a hint of history in it because it is an opportunity for the director to give their point of view telling a chapter in time to all of us and that there may be a lesson in it. This is not my preamble to say that I know what the story tells but it's for each of us to either see it as it is or what it reminds each of you about where we've come from and where we are now in the world. Times were very very difficult in the 1000s.

I recommend that everyone at least give it your sincere chance to let this stylized version breathe and know that it was done with care so as not to bore us with all the intricate in between details. It's entertaining, and that is all it is, part of history, and not the whole. It is done thoughtfully, without being stretched and drawn out.

It's a shame that when I read the reviews that are lesser than three I hear the proverbial sound of the breaking glass of society that has mutated everything possible, that there is something wrong with anything that is not on their side. It is my opinion that everyone should look at everything and everybody for each side it represents and not expect it to be your way and your belief alone. This is sort of what I seen in the retelling of this historical drama. Two sides of society, warring with each other, one taking control the other one not pleased with the outcome and then trying to retaliate constantly. We have not come very far from what we see in this story and that is a shame. It's an utter shame.

If you respect cinema and a director's opinion on history and it wakes you up to read a book to learn more of the details that actually happened then I think you should see this series from a director did their job well.

The show feels like a weak attempt to replicate Game of Thrones, but lacks the complexity and craftsmanship that made it compelling - I wasn't particularly excited about King and Conqueror, but since the pilot dropped, I decided to give it a try. Unfortunately, it didn't take long to realize how poorly written it is.

1. Pacing and Setting The timeline and geography make no sense. Characters jump from Normandy to England, from Wessex to Mercia, then back to London and Normandy in what feels like minutes. Journeys that should realistically take days are treated like quick strolls, which kills immersion.

2. Weak Characters I understand it's only the pilot, and I don't expect to fall in love with characters right away. But here, the problem isn't attachment-it's that the characters are written poorly to begin with. They feel shallow, rushed, and lack any real personality. Even the action scenes feel like noise without purpose.

3. "Tell, Don't Show" Writing Instead of letting the story unfold naturally, the script spoon-feeds the audience with clumsy exposition. We're told outright: "this is his brother," "this is his cousin," "this man did him a favor," "this is his half-brother." It's lazy writing that underestimates viewers' intelligence.

4. Unrealistic Politics I'm no politician, but I'm certain that's not how politics works. The way power struggles, alliances, and negotiations are written feels cartoonish and completely detached from reality.

Final Thought As a pilot, it fails at its most important job making me want to watch more.

Horrible Lighting Larping & Historical Inaccurate - If King and Conqueror set out to prove that history, character, and artistry could all be butchered in one fell swoop, then mission accomplished. Ignore the 10 star bots this series misses on all fronts

Lighting: Dark for All the Wrong Reasons

The series seems to believe that murky shadows equal "gritty realism." Instead, viewers are left squinting at their screens, trying to distinguish characters from the set pieces. What should have been a sweeping, visually commanding epic turns into a dimly lit slog that feels more like watching a candle slowly burn out than a high-budget production.

Casting: Wooden and Mismatched

The casting is, to put it mildly, a disaster. Leads lack presence, charisma, or even basic believability. Rather than embodying figures of historical magnitude, they stumble through their lines like stand-ins waiting for the real actors to arrive. Chemistry between characters is nonexistent, leaving every supposed moment of tension or romance flatter than a parchment scroll.

Historical Inaccuracies: A Slap in the Face

History isn't a mere suggestion, yet King and Conqueror treats it as optional fanfiction. Dates blur, events are wildly rearranged, and characters spout 21st-century attitudes that would've gotten them executed in the era they supposedly inhabit. Any claim to being "based on true events" is laughable-this is more Once Upon a Time in History Class than an actual depiction of the past.

Dialogue: Wooden, Clunky, and Groan-Inducing

The script feels like it was run through a medieval phrase generator and then stripped of all poetry or nuance. Exchanges meant to cut deep land with a dull thud. Instead of commanding authority, the dialogue reduces kings to bumbling bureaucrats and warriors to grumpy LARPers. At best, it's unintentionally funny; at worst, it's unbearable.

Final Verdict

King and Conqueror manages to fumble every element it touches. Where there should be majesty, there is monotony. Where there should be accuracy, there is arrogance. And where there should be soul, there is only shadow.

avis:
Travesty - Could we blame the budget for this disaster? Perhaps. The battle scenes clearly swallowed the lion's share, but once the dust settled, the rest of the production limped along on scraps. Villages look like backlots, interiors have all the warmth of a discount costume drama, and the script feels as if it was scribbled on the back of a pub napkin between Google searches.

Historical fact-checking? Non-existent. The writers seem to have treated a thousand years of history as optional reading, which is bold considering the story they are telling is one of the most famous events in British and European history. Instead, we are given a cut-and-paste aesthetic, as though someone raided the leftover wardrobe from Vikings and hoped no one would notice.

Even the basics of appearance are wrong. The Normans, historically clean shaven, are shown here with shaggy beards, while the Saxons, famous for their moustaches, are curiously deprived of them. A single glance at the Bayeux Tapestry would have put that right. Noblewomen, meanwhile, are costumed as bedraggled peasants, hair loose and dresses plain. In reality, they would have looked impeccable, with fine gowns and covered hair. These were women of rank, not extras dragged in from a muddy village scene.

Performances from James Norton and Nikolaj Coster-Waldau fail to portray any sense of urgency or realism in their characters' fight for the crown. Instead, they seem pedestrian throughout, merely going through the paces as if on autopilot. For a story defined by high stakes and bitter conflict, this lack of dramatic weight is fatal.

One also feels the heavy hand of American involvement dragging the whole enterprise down. Rather than trusting historians and creatives with expertise in this period, there is a sense of arrogant, top-down instruction that dictated the route forward. The result is a series that is neither accurate nor compelling, shaped by misguided assumptions and easy choices that miss the mark entirely.

The direction is equally uninspired, offering nothing but safe, predictable camera angles that might generously be described as "student film chic". It is not just inaccuracy, it is laziness. When an audience sits down to watch this period, they deserve ambition, texture, and a sense of truth. Instead, we are served a bland casserole of clichés. Even the dialogue clunks, occasionally wandering into anachronisms so glaring you wonder if the writers had Wikipedia open in one tab and a medieval fantasy role-play forum in the other.

After twenty years of ignoring the nagging suggestion to create an IMDb account, I finally caved, solely to gift this sorry mess a two-star rating. That is how passionately disgruntled I am.

And for anyone still unsure: "Your Majesty" was not heard in the 11th century. It was first used at the court of Henry VIII, half a millennium later. A slip like that says it all.

It was only in around the 18th century, when the horse-racing industry got going, that folk started breeding them so they'd be 12 feet long, 10 feet high, and with legs that are prone to snapping if they so much as look upon a pebble.

Okay, that's that out of the way.

'King and Conqueror' (the first episode, which was all I could stand) was just awful. I've nothing good to say about it ... except the stuff about the horses.

avis:
Well..... - I'm certain I'm writing a review mostly women will relate to so here goes.

I love period dramas and even documentaries. What I hate are period dramas either written as documentaries where historical facts are focused on and characterization, interactions and story telling are completely thrown to the wayside or a combo documentary/ period drama where historical facts are Willy nilly, interactions between lovers and spouses are focused totally on whatever war is currently happening or planned and you are introduced to so many characters in the first 5 minutes it takes you to episode 5 to figure out who is who and what relationship they have unless you're a history scholar. This series is option two.

It has very good acting( love seeing you Jamie Lannister ) and cinematography. However, I had to use Google to try to figure out who everyone was as each family was given about a 4 minute initial scene then it moved on to another family with almost identical clothing and uniforms, accents, etc. So basically you're in utter confusion the first several episodes.

Then we come to the relationships. Yes they portray all the women as strong, ruthless and usually smarter than the men. According to history a few of them were but not all and considering the patriarchal time period and the origin cultures/telgions at least a few would have been fairly uneducated and focused solely on motherhood and hearth. There was no chemistry between any of the couples, none, even though per history a few had a great love and the men had no history of bastard children, but no romance at all.

As far as the male characterizations they all were as alike as a loaf of white bread. Even Sveyn who was portrayed as somewhat of a rabble rouser never showed the type of true rebellion and difference in character from everyone else you'd expect.

All in all the series lacked true passion and investment. This was an amazing time in history where everyone basically grew up in war zones. IRL this forged extremely strong, dynamic leaders yet even William comes across as middle of the road making you wonder just what made him the victor over all the rest,

avis:
Historical inaccuracies - The historical inaccuracies in King and Conqueror are honestly mind-blowing. I understand that historical dramas take creative liberties, but this goes far beyond that. Key events are altered or completely ignored, timelines are a mess, and characters behave in ways that make absolutely no sense if you know even basic history.

It feels less like a historical story and more like a fantasy loosely borrowing real names. You end up spending more time questioning what's on screen than actually enjoying the plot. At some point you have to wonder how the director and writers looked at this and thought it was acceptable.

If you're someone who cares even slightly about historical accuracy, be prepared for a lot of frustration. Visually it has moments, but the constant inaccuracies make it very hard to take seriously.
